E1A01: A USB signal sits above its carrier, so a 3 kHz signal on 14.348 MHz reaches 14.348 + 0.003 = 14.351 MHz. The 20-meter band ends at 14.350 MHz, so the top 1 kHz of the signal falls outside the band even though the carrier itself is inside [97.301, 97.307(b)].
E1A02: LSB energy lies below the displayed carrier, roughly 3 kHz down. Setting the carrier at least 3 kHz above the lower band edge keeps the whole sideband inside the band; any lower setting would push part of the signal past the edge [97.301, 97.307(b)].
E1A03: Data on 20 meters is allowed up to 14.150 MHz, and a USB data signal extends above its carrier. Highest carrier = 14.150 MHz minus 2.8 kHz = 14.1500 - 0.0028 = 14.1472 MHz, which keeps the top of the signal at the segment edge [97.305(c), 97.307(f)(3)].
E1A04: The Extra class phone segment on 75 meters starts at 3.600 MHz. An LSB signal with its carrier at 3.601 MHz spreads about 3 kHz lower, down to roughly 3.598 MHz, so part of it lands in the CW and data segment [97.301(b), 97.305(c)].
E1A05: A station aboard a US documented or registered vessel or craft may transmit only when the apparatus is under the physical control of someone named in an amateur license grant or authorized for alien reciprocal operation. No marine radio license or commercial permit is involved [97.5(a)(2)].
E1A06: On the five 60-meter channels a CW signal must be transmitted on the channel's center frequency. Phone, data and RTTY may set the carrier 1.5 kHz below center instead, but CW goes right in the middle [97.303(h)(3)].
E1A07: In the 2200-meter band (135.7 to 137.8 kHz) the radiated power limit is 1 watt EIRP, alongside a 1.5 kW PEP transmitter limit. Because antennas this low are so inefficient, the radiated figure is the one that matters [97.313(k)].
E1A08: In a message forwarding system, the control operator of the station that originated the message is primarily accountable for any rule violation in it. Forwarding stations that pass it along inadvertently are not held accountable, though they must stop once they learn of it [97.219(b)].
E1A09: In the 630-meter band (472 to 479 kHz) stations are limited to 5 watts EIRP and 500 W PEP. Stations in Alaska within 800 km of Russia are held to 1 watt EIRP, which is why the question excludes parts of Alaska [97.313(l)].
E1A10: Before an amateur station on a ship or aircraft is operated, its installation and operation must be approved by the ship's master or the aircraft's pilot in command. The rules set no requirement for a separate power supply or special band segments [97.11(a)].
E1A11: Any FCC-issued amateur license lets you operate aboard a US-registered vessel in international waters, within the privileges of your license class. There is no marine or aircraft endorsement and no minimum class requirement [97.5(a)(2)].
E1B01: A spurious emission is energy outside the necessary bandwidth that can be reduced or removed without affecting the information being sent, such as harmonics or parasitics. It is defined by what it is, not by whether it happens to cause interference [97.3(a)(43)].
E1B02: On HF, a non-phone emission may not be wider than a communications quality phone signal of the same modulation type. Digital voice and SSTV in an SSB-sized channel therefore stay within about 3 kHz; 10 kHz and wider would be far too broad [97.307(f)(2)].
E1B03: An amateur station within 1600 meters, about 1 mile, of an FCC monitoring facility must protect it from harmful interference. Failing to do so can lead to operating restrictions [97.13(b)].
E1B04: Amateurs on 70 centimeters are secondary to US Government radiolocation systems, so they must not cause harmful interference to them. If a repeater does, its control operator must stop transmitting or change the repeater so the interference ends [97.303(b)].
E1B05: The National Radio Quiet Zone is an area of Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia around the National Radio Astronomy Observatory at Green Bank. Stations there must coordinate certain operations to protect radio astronomy [97.3(a)(33)].
E1B06: Antenna structures near a public use airport, or taller than 200 feet, may require notice to the FAA and registration with the FCC under Part 17. The EPA and airport zoning boards play no role in that Part 97 requirement [97.15(a)].
E1B07: PRB-1 is the FCC ruling that limits how far state and local governments, through zoning and similar ordinances, can restrict amateur antennas. It does not reach private agreements such as homeowners association rules [97.15(b)].
E1B08: When an amateur station causes general interference to broadcast reception on well-designed receivers, the FCC may require the station to avoid transmitting on the offending frequencies during certain hours. A total shutdown or a whole-band ban is not what the rule provides [97.121(a)].
E1B09: Any FCC-licensed primary, club or military recreation station may transmit in RACES once it is certified, or registered, by the civil defense organization for the area it serves. License class is not the test [97.407(a)].
E1B10: A station operating under RACES may use all amateur frequencies and emissions authorized to its control operator, shared with normal amateur use. Restrictions apply only if the President invokes War Emergency Powers [97.407(b)].
E1B11: PRB-1 does not let amateurs put up any antenna they like. It requires state and local rules to reasonably accommodate amateur communications and to use the minimum practicable regulation to meet a legitimate purpose [97.15(b)].
E1C01: Any emission on 60 meters, whether on the four channels or in the 5351.5 to 5366.5 kHz segment, must not occupy more than 2.8 kHz. That width fits a standard SSB-sized data signal [97.303(h)(3)].
E1C02: Transmissions to amateurs in other countries must be limited to communications incidental to the purposes of the amateur service and remarks of a personal nature. English is not required, and third party traffic rules depend on agreements with each country [97.117].
E1C03: After notifying the Utilities Technology Council of call sign, band and antenna coordinates, a station may begin operating on 2200 or 630 meters when 30 days pass, unless UTC says the site is within 1 km of a power line carrier system on those frequencies [97.303(g)(2)].
E1C04: An IARP, or International Amateur Radio Permit, is a document under the Inter-American Convention that lets licensed amateurs from member countries operate in other participating countries in the Americas without a separate license [97.3(a)(24)].
E1C05: A station under automatic control may pass third party communications only when transmitting RTTY or data emissions. Voice, SSB and CW third party traffic require a control operator at a control point [97.115(c)].
E1C06: To operate under CEPT rules abroad, a US licensee must carry a copy of FCC Public Notice DA 16-1048, which explains the CEPT arrangement, along with proof of US citizenship and the FCC license. No embassy approval is needed.
E1C07: Before transmitting on 630 or 2200 meters, an operator must notify the Utilities Technology Council of the call sign, the band or bands, and the coordinates of the fixed antenna location. The FAA and the Department of the Interior are not involved [97.303(g)(2)].
E1C08: A remotely controlled station must have a way to limit its transmissions to no more than 3 minutes if the control link fails. This stops a runaway transmitter from staying on the air indefinitely [97.213(b)].
E1C09: For frequency or phase modulation below 29.0 MHz, the modulation index at the highest modulating frequency may not exceed 1.0. Keeping the index low keeps FM signals narrow in the crowded HF bands [97.307(f)(1)].
E1C10: For transmitters installed after January 1, 2003, any spurious emission on a frequency below 30 MHz must be at least 43 dB below the mean power of the fundamental. A level of -43 dB is the minimum attenuation required [97.307(d)].
E1C11: Under CEPT Recommendation T/R 61-01, US citizens with FCC licenses can operate in many European countries, and licensees from CEPT countries can operate in the US. The IARP covers countries of the Americas instead [97.107].
E1C12: Phone and image emissions are authorized across the entire 630-meter band, 472 to 479 kHz, as are RTTY and data. There is no separate CW-only or data-only segment there [97.305(c)].
E1D01: Telemetry is a one-way transmission of measurements made at a distance from the measuring instrument, such as a balloon sending back temperature readings. A one-way signal that starts or stops a device's functions is telecommand, not telemetry [97.3(a)(46)].
E1D02: A space telecommand station may send special codes intended to obscure the meaning of telecommand messages to a space station, to keep others from taking control of a satellite. Repeater control links and mesh nodes have no such permission [97.211(b)].
E1D03: A telecommand station is an amateur station that sends communications to initiate, modify or terminate functions of a space station. A station on Earth working other stations through satellites is an Earth station instead [97.3(a)(45)].
E1D04: A balloon-borne telemetry station is not a space station or telecommand station, so like most stations it must transmit its assigned call sign to identify itself. Power and grid locator are not required in the identification [97.119(a)].
E1D05: A station under telecommand on or within 50 km of Earth must have a photocopy of its license posted conspicuously, plus a label with the name, address and telephone number of the licensee and of at least one designated control operator. Each listed item is required [97.213(d)].
E1D06: A station sending control signals to a model craft such as a plane or boat must not exceed 1 watt of transmitter power. Those control signals are not treated as codes meant to obscure meaning [97.215(c)].
E1D07: Space stations may use HF segments at 7.0 to 7.1 MHz and 14.00 to 14.25 MHz, plus the 15-meter and 10-meter bands (and 17 and 12 meters as well). Thirty meters is not among them, and not every HF band is open to satellites [97.207(c)].
E1D08: The only VHF space station allocation is the 144 to 146 MHz portion of the 2-meter band. Six meters and 1.25 meters have no space station segments [97.207(c)(2)].
E1D09: On UHF, space stations are authorized at 435 to 438 MHz in the 70-centimeter band and 2400 to 2450 MHz in the 13-centimeter band. The 33-centimeter band has no space station segment [97.207(c)(2)].
E1D10: Any amateur station that the space station licensee designates may act as a telecommand station for that satellite, within its control operator's privileges. Neither AMSAT nor the ITU makes that designation [97.211(a)].
E1D11: Any amateur station may be an Earth station, and an operator of any license class may be its control operator, limited to that class's privileges. No special course or higher class is required [97.209(a)].
E1D12: Space stations, beacon stations and telecommand stations are all allowed to make one-way transmissions. Repeaters and message forwarding stations carry two-way traffic and get no such general permission [97.207(e), 97.203(g), 97.211(d)].
E1E01: VEs and VECs may be reimbursed by examinees only for out-of-pocket expenses incurred in preparing, processing, administering or coordinating an amateur license exam. Teaching classes or selling study materials are not covered expenses [97.527].
E1E02: The VECs together maintain one question pool for each written exam element, and each pool must hold at least 10 times the questions used on a single exam. The FCC does not write the pools [97.523].
E1E03: A Volunteer Examiner Coordinator is an organization with a written agreement with the FCC to coordinate amateur license exams. Individual volunteers are VEs, not VECs [97.521].
E1E04: A licensee becomes a VE only when a VEC accredits them after confirming they meet FCC requirements. Holding a General or higher license does not make anyone a VE automatically, and the FCC does not accredit VEs directly [97.509(b)(1), 97.525].
E1E05: When an examinee does not pass an element, the administering VEs must return the application document to the examinee and tell them the grade. Nothing is sent to the FCC for a failed attempt [97.509(j)].
E1E06: Every administering VE is responsible for the proper conduct and necessary supervision of the exam, and each must observe the examinee throughout. That duty is not left to a single session manager or to the VEC [97.509(c)].
E1E07: Examinees must follow the VEs' instructions, and the administering VEs must immediately end the exam of a candidate who fails to comply. A warning is not what the rule requires, and other candidates are not affected [97.509(c), 97.511].
E1E08: A VE may not give an exam to listed relatives, including a spouse, children, parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, step relatives and in-laws. Friends and employees are not on the list [97.509(d)].
E1E09: A VE who administers or certifies an exam by fraudulent means may have their station license grant revoked and their operator license grant suspended. The rule names those license penalties, not a fine or prison term [97.509(e)].
E1E10: After a successful exam, the administering VEs send the application document to the coordinating VEC as that VEC instructs. The VEC, not the VE team or the applicant, files with the FCC [97.509(m)].
E1E11: When an examinee passes every element needed for a new license or upgrade, three VEs must certify that the examinee is qualified and that they followed the administering VE rules. VEs do not issue licenses themselves [97.509(i)].
E1F01: Spread spectrum emissions are authorized only in the 222 to 225 MHz segment of 1.25 meters and on higher bands, where the emission table lists SS. Below 222 MHz, including 2 meters, SS is not allowed [97.305(c)].
E1F02: A Canadian amateur in the US operates under the terms of the US and Canada convention and the conditions of the Canadian license, but never beyond the privileges of a US Amateur Extra license. No US license is needed [97.107(a)].
E1F03: Uncertified amplifiers capable of operation below 144 MHz may not be built or modified by non-amateurs. One exception covers amplifiers constructed or modified by a licensed amateur for use at an amateur station, so a dealer may sell one of those [97.315(b)(1)].
E1F04: Line A runs roughly parallel to the US and Canada border on the US side, from Aberdeen, Washington, east to Maine. North of it, some UHF frequencies are limited to protect Canadian services [97.3(a)(30)].
E1F05: Stations in the contiguous US north of Line A may not transmit in the 420 to 430 MHz segment, which Canada uses for other services. The 440 to 450 MHz part of 70 centimeters is still available there [97.303(m)(1)].
E1F06: The FCC may grant a Special Temporary Authority so an amateur station can carry out experimental communications not otherwise covered by the rules. Special event call signs and exam sessions are handled through other processes [1.931].
E1F07: An amateur may send a message to a business, such as ordering a pizza, as long as neither the operator nor the operator's employer has a pecuniary interest in the communication. No dollar threshold appears in the rules [97.113(a)(3)].
E1F08: Amateur stations may not transmit communications for hire or for material compensation, direct or indirect, except where the rules allow it. Political or religious content and non-English languages are not prohibited [97.113(a)(2)].
E1F09: Mesh networks follow the same Part 97 content rules, so messages encoded to obscure their meaning cannot be sent. Email and third party traffic are permitted when handled under the normal rules [97.113(a)(4)].
E1F10: Any Technician, General, Advanced or Amateur Extra licensee may be the control operator of an auxiliary station, within that class's privileges. Every current license class qualifies, so it is not limited to General and above [97.201(a)].
E1F11: To be certified, an amplifier must meet the spurious emission standards when operated at the lesser of 1.5 kW PEP or its full output power. The rules also cap its gain at 15 dB, so 23 dB would be too much [97.317(a)(1)].
E2A01: An ascending pass is the part of an orbit where the satellite is moving northward, so it crosses your sky from south to north. On a descending pass it travels from north to south.
E2A02: An inverting linear transponder mixes the uplink with a local oscillator and sends the difference. That flips the passband, so signals swap positions and USB comes down as LSB, and because the uplink and downlink Doppler shifts move in opposite directions, the net shift is reduced. All of these are true.
E2A03: The uplink passband is mixed with a local oscillator, and the difference frequency is amplified and transmitted. Taking the difference, rather than the sum, is what turns the passband upside down. The signal is never demodulated and remodulated.
E2A04: A satellite's mode tells you which bands it listens and transmits on, such as a 2-meter uplink with a 70-centimeter downlink. It says nothing about the orbit type or how the satellite is pointed.
E2A05: The letters in a mode designator name the frequency bands used: one letter for the uplink and one for the downlink. For example, U/V means a UHF uplink and a VHF downlink. Power and polarization are not part of it.
E2A06: Keplerian elements are the set of numbers, such as inclination, eccentricity and mean motion, that describe a satellite's orbit. Tracking programs use them to predict where the satellite will be and when it will pass overhead.
E2A07: A linear transponder repeats everything in its passband faithfully, so any mode that fits can pass through it: FM, CW, SSB, SSTV, PSK and packet among them. Linear transponders are usually used for SSB and CW, but all these choices are correct.
E2A08: A linear transponder divides its limited output power among every signal in its passband. A station that runs too much uplink power takes a bigger share and lowers the downlink strength for everyone else using the satellite.
E2A09: In satellite mode names, L band is the 23-centimeter band (around 1.2 GHz) and S band is the 13-centimeter band (around 2.4 GHz). The 2-meter and 70-centimeter bands are V and U.
E2A10: A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator once per day in the same direction Earth turns, about 35,800 km up, so it seems to hang still in the sky. Low earth orbit and highly elliptical satellites move across the sky.
E2A11: Spin modulation and Faraday rotation keep changing a signal's polarization, which makes a linearly polarized antenna fade in and out. A circularly polarized antenna responds about equally to any linear orientation, so those fades are much smaller.
E2A12: A store-and-forward satellite receives digital messages, holds them in memory, and downloads them later, often when it passes over the recipient. This lets stations exchange traffic without both being in view of the satellite at the same time.
E2B01: A coding rate of 3/4 means 3 of every 4 bits carry data and 1 is added for forward error correction. One bit out of four is 1/4, or 25% of the data sent. It has nothing to do with compression or guard intervals.
E2B02: An NTSC frame is made of 525 horizontal lines, sent as two interlaced fields of 262.5 lines each, 30 frames per second. 1080 lines belongs to high definition digital formats.
E2B03: Interlacing sends the odd-numbered lines in one field and the even-numbered lines in the next field. The two fields mesh into one frame, giving smooth motion without doubling the bandwidth.
E2B04: Analog SSTV sends color by transmitting each color component, such as red, green and blue or luminance and color difference, as its own scan line in sequence. The receiver then combines them into one color line. There is no color subcarrier or burst.
E2B05: In fast-scan TV, most of the lower sideband is filtered off, leaving only a vestige near the carrier. This saves bandwidth, and the vestige keeps the low frequency video components accurate, which complete removal of the sideband would disturb.
E2B06: Vestigial sideband is amplitude modulation in which one sideband is sent in full and only part of the other sideband remains. It sits between double sideband AM and single sideband in bandwidth.
E2B07: DVB-T, the digital TV standard amateurs use, carries its data on OFDM subcarriers modulated with QPSK or QAM. FM, FSK, AM and on-off keying are not used for DVB-T.
E2B08: Parts of the 70-centimeter band line up with cable TV channels, so an ordinary cable-ready analog TV tuned to those channels can receive amateur fast-scan TV. Channel 2 is not in the 70-centimeter band at all.
E2B09: DRM digital SSTV fits in a voice channel, so an ordinary SSB receiver feeds the audio to a computer, and software decodes the picture. AM, CDMA and AREDN mesh gear are not used to receive it.
E2B10: In analog SSTV, brightness is coded by the audio tone's frequency, from about 1500 Hz for black up to about 2300 Hz for white. Tone amplitude does not carry picture information.
E2B11: The VIS code is a short digital burst at the start of an SSTV image that tells the receiving software which SSTV mode follows, so it can decode the picture correctly. It does not carry the call sign or provide line sync.
E2B12: Each SSTV line starts with a sync pulse at a specific tone frequency, usually 1200 Hz, below the range used for picture brightness. The receiving software detects that tone to start the next line.
E2C01: When a US licensee operates a remote station located in the US, the normal call sign is enough and no indicator is required. State abbreviations or district suffixes are not called for by the rules [97.119].
E2C02: ADIF, the Amateur Data Interchange Format, is the standard file format for moving log data between logging programs and services such as QSL and award systems. NEC is an antenna modeling program, not a log format.
E2C03: Contests are generally not held on 30 meters, one of the WARC bands, by long-standing practice. Six meters, 70 centimeters and 33 centimeters are all used in VHF and UHF contests.
E2C04: Amateur mesh networks usually run on frequencies around 2.4 and 5.8 GHz that amateurs share with unlicensed Wi-Fi and other data services. That overlap lets modified Wi-Fi routers serve as amateur mesh nodes.
E2C05: A DX QSL manager handles QSL card confirmations for a DX station, receiving requests and sending out the cards or electronic confirmations. This frees the DX operator, often on a busy expedition, to stay on the air.
E2C06: In VHF and UHF contests, SSB and CW activity gathers in the weak signal segment of each band, mostly near the calling frequency such as 50.125 or 144.200 MHz. The top and middle of the bands carry FM and repeater traffic.
E2C07: Cabrillo is a standard text format for submitting contest logs electronically. Contest sponsors process the logs with it to check contacts and calculate scores. It is a file format, not a contest exchange or rule set.
E2C08: Logbook of The World matches confirmations from both stations electronically, for contacts within the US, between US and non-US stations, and for awards such as Worked All States. All these choices are correct.
E2C09: Amateur mesh networks are usually built from commercial wireless routers loaded with custom firmware, such as AREDN, that runs them under amateur rules. Two-meter packet radio and EchoLink are different systems.
E2C10: DX stations often work split: they transmit on one frequency and listen on another. This keeps the crowd of callers off the DX frequency, reduces interference, raises the contact rate, and lets them transmit where some callers cannot. Each of these is true.
E2C11: In a pileup or contest, send your full call sign once or twice and then listen. Partial calls slow things down, and repeating the DX station's call wastes time because the DX operator already knows it.
E2C12: Latency is the time delay between an operator's action, such as keying, and the matching change in the transmitted signal. It is a concern in remote operation over the internet. Jitter is variation in delay, not the delay itself.
E2D01: MSK144 is a WSJT-X mode built for meteor scatter. Its short, fast transmissions can be decoded from the brief pings when signals bounce off meteor trails. WSPR is for weak signal beacons and APRS for position reporting.
E2D02: In VHF contests using FT8 or FT4, the exchange includes the grid square instead of a signal-to-noise report, since contest scoring is based on grid squares and distance.
E2D03: Q65 is a WSJT-X mode designed for very weak signals, including earth-moon-earth paths, and can average several transmissions to dig out a signal. MSK144 is meant for meteor scatter instead.
E2D04: APRS is used to track amateur balloons in real time: the balloon sends GPS position packets that are picked up and relayed by digipeaters and internet gateways, then shown on maps.
E2D05: JT65 is built to decode signals with a very low signal-to-noise ratio, well below what the ear can hear, using long transmissions and strong error correction. The 65 refers to the number of tones, not its bandwidth or speed.
E2D06: EME stations usually take turns on a fixed schedule, transmitting and receiving in synchronized time periods such as alternating minutes or shorter digital cycles. Each station knows exactly when to listen for the very weak echo.
E2D07: APRS runs over AX.25, the amateur packet radio link layer protocol. PACTOR and AMTOR are HF ARQ modes, and QAM is a modulation method, not a protocol.
E2D08: APRS beacons are sent as AX.25 Unnumbered Information frames, which need no connection or acknowledgment. Any station can receive and decode them, which suits one-to-many position reports.
E2D09: JT65 uses multitone AFSK: an audio signal steps among 65 different tones to send its symbols. It is not phase shift keying or quadrature amplitude modulation.
E2D10: In WIDE3-1, the first number is the number of digipeater hops requested and the second is how many remain. Each digipeater reduces the second number by one, so WIDE3-1 shows three hops asked for with one left.
E2D11: APRS stations pass data along through packet digipeaters, which receive a packet and retransmit it to extend its range. DMR and C4FM repeaters carry digital voice, not APRS packets.
E2E01: Data emissions on HF are most commonly sent with frequency shift keying, as in RTTY and many digital modes. Spread spectrum and pulse modulation are not allowed below 30 MHz, and DTMF over FM is a VHF signaling method.
E2E02: WSJT-X modes such as FT8 transmit and receive in fixed time slots, so the computer clocks at both stations must be synchronized, usually within a second, from internet time or GPS. Without that, decodes fail.
E2E03: FT4 uses 4-tone continuous-phase frequency shift keying, which is where the 4 in its name comes from. Its transmit and receive periods are 7.5 seconds each, not four per minute.
E2E04: FST4 uses four-tone Gaussian frequency shift keying, offers several transmit and receive period lengths, and has seven tone spacings to suit different conditions. All these choices are correct.
E2E05: WSPR sends only short beacon messages with a call sign, grid and power level for propagation studies. It cannot carry typed conversation, while RTTY, PSK31 and MFSK16 all support keyboard-to-keyboard chat.
E2E06: FT8 runs in 15-second cycles, about 12.6 seconds of transmission plus time for decoding. Stations alternate in fixed even and odd periods, so one cycle is 15 seconds.
E2E07: Q65 can average several receive cycles of a repeated message, which helps pull very weak signals out of the noise on paths like EME. That is the key difference from JT65 among these, not keyboard chat or quadrature modulation.
E2E08: PACTOR is an ARQ mode with error correction that can transfer binary files and email without errors. PSK31 and RTTY are keyboard modes, and AMTOR carries only text characters.
E2E09: PSK31 uses Varicode, a variable-length character code in which common letters get shorter bit patterns, like Morse code. RTTY uses fixed five-bit Baudot codes.
E2E10: An FT8 signal is only about 50 Hz wide, narrower than MFSK16 (about 316 Hz), 170 Hz shift RTTY (about 250 Hz), or PACTOR IV (about 2.4 kHz).
E2E11: Direct FSK shifts the transmitter's VFO itself between mark and space frequencies. Audio FSK instead feeds audio tones into an SSB transmitter's microphone input. Bandwidth and speed are about the same either way.
E2E12: ALE radios keep scanning a list of frequencies and sound calls. When one hears its designated call sign, it stops, sounds an alert, and links on the best channel, so operators do not have to hunt for a working frequency.
E2E13: PACTOR IV uses adaptive high-speed modulation with error correction in about a 2.4 kHz channel, giving the most data throughput when conditions are clear. FT8, RTTY and MFSK16 are far slower.
E0A01: A ground rod or external earth connection gives lightning a low-impedance path to dissipate its charge into the earth outside the building. It does not cure RF problems between pieces of equipment.
E0A02: A neighbor's home is not under your control and the people there may not know about RF exposure, so you must use the uncontrolled, general population limits, which are stricter. The term is maximum permissible exposure, not emission.
E0A03: The FCC exposure limits are lowest in the 30 to 300 MHz range because the human body absorbs RF most strongly there, near its whole-body resonance. Limits relax above and below that range.
E0A04: At a multi-transmitter site where the total exposure limit is exceeded, every transmitter that contributes 5 percent or more of its own MPE limit in that area shares responsibility for fixing the problem.
E0A05: At microwave frequencies, compact antennas can have very high gain, concentrating power into a narrow beam. Standing in or near that beam can expose a person to high RF levels. Microwaves are not ionizing radiation.
E0A06: Below 300 MHz, the body responds to both the electric and magnetic fields, the two fields can peak at different locations, especially in the near field, and reflections make field strength vary from place to place. Each of these is true, so both limits are needed.
E0A07: 100% tie-off means the climber always has at least one lanyard attached to the tower. When moving past an obstacle, the second lanyard is connected before the first is released, so there is never a moment without fall protection.
E0A08: SAR, the specific absorption rate, measures how fast RF energy is absorbed by body tissue, in watts per kilogram. It is the basis for many exposure limits, especially for portable radios.
E0A09: Under the FCC rules that took effect in 2021, hand-held transceivers sold before May 3, 2021 are exempt from RF exposure evaluations. Low power alone or near-field operation does not create an exemption.
E0A10: Under the current FCC rules, every amateur station on every band, 80 meters included, must perform an RF exposure evaluation, at least to see whether it is exempt. The old blanket exemptions based on power level or mode no longer apply.
E0A11: Lanyards should attach to the tower legs, the strongest structural members. Masts, guy brackets and rungs may not be built to hold the force of a fall.
E0A12: A shock-absorbing lanyard should be connected above head level, so a fall is short and the absorber has enough length to work. Clipping in low lets the climber drop farther before it catches.
E3A01: Earth-moon-earth works whenever both stations can see the moon at the same time, so they can be roughly half the planet apart, about 12,000 miles along the surface. Perigee or apogee changes path loss slightly, not how far apart the stations may be.
E3A02: Libration is the slight rocking of the moon as seen from Earth, so the echo comes back from many points on its rough surface whose path lengths keep shifting. Those reflections add and cancel, giving a rapid, fluttery, irregular fade rather than a slow change.
E3A03: Path loss on an EME circuit grows with distance, and the moon is closest to Earth at perigee, so the round trip is shortest then and losses are about 2 dB lower than at apogee. A full moon adds sky noise but does not shorten the path.
E3A04: A radio wave moves at right angles to both its electric and magnetic fields, in the direction given by their cross product. It never travels along either field, and its direction does not depend on the phase of either one.
E3A05: In a radio wave the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other, and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel. In free space they are in phase, so being 90 degrees out of phase is not the description.
E3A06: When darkness lowers the maximum usable frequency below your operating frequency, the signal stops being refracted back to Earth over that path. Moving down to a lower HF band brings you back under the new, lower MUF so the contact can continue.
E3A07: Microwave ducts form where a layer of warm, dry air sits over cooler, moist air, a temperature inversion that is common over large bodies of water. The sharp change in refractive index traps and guides the signal for long distances.
E3A08: Meteors burn up at roughly 50 to 75 miles altitude, which is the E region, leaving a short-lived trail of ionized gas there. Signals bounce off that trail, which is why meteor scatter paths match single-hop E-layer distances.
E3A09: Meteor trails reflect best at low VHF, so 28 MHz through 148 MHz, covering 10, 6 and 2 meters, is the most useful range. Lower HF is already handled by the normal ionosphere, and at 220 to 450 MHz the trails reflect far less energy.
E3A10: Speed in a medium is v = c / n, where n is the index of refraction. A higher index means slower travel, which is also why a wave bends when it passes between materials with different indexes.
E3A11: Tropospheric ducts commonly carry microwave signals about 100 to 300 miles, far beyond line of sight. Much longer duct paths happen now and then, but a few thousand miles is not the typical range.
E3A12: Auroral propagation comes from intense ionization in the auroral zone when charged particles from the Sun pour into the upper atmosphere, which happens during severe geomagnetic storms. Quiet geomagnetic conditions produce little or no aurora.
E3A13: Signals reflected from the moving aurora are smeared by Doppler spread and sound raspy and distorted, so voice and RTTY become hard to copy. CW keeps working because the operator only needs to hear the tone come and go, and it fits a narrow bandwidth.
E3A14: In a circularly polarized wave the electric and magnetic fields rotate around the direction of travel, making one full turn each cycle. The field is not bent into a circle, and the name has nothing to do with waves circling Earth.
E3B01: TEP links stations roughly 2,000 to 3,000 miles apart on a path that crosses the geomagnetic equator at about a right angle, such as the southern US to South America. The stations sit at similar distances north and south of that equator.
E3B02: Transequatorial propagation can reach about 5,000 miles, well past a normal single F-layer hop of about 2,500 miles. It uses the dense ionization bulges on either side of the geomagnetic equator to cover the path.
E3B03: TEP is most likely in the afternoon and early evening, when the equatorial ionization built up during the day is at its strongest. By late at night or early morning the effect has usually faded.
E3B04: As a radio wave enters the ionosphere, Earth's magnetic field splits it into two waves, the ordinary and extraordinary, each elliptically polarized and each propagating on its own path. The names have nothing to do with how far they skip.
E3B05: On 160 meters the D layer absorbs signals heavily in daylight, so long-distance contacts work best when the whole path between the stations is in darkness. Once sunlight touches any part of the path, the signal usually disappears.
E3B06: Long-path contacts, the long way around the globe, show up most often on 40 and 20 meters. Those bands can follow a long path that stays along the gray line or in darkness, while 160 and 80 suffer too much absorption and the higher bands often lack the ionization.
E3B07: A lower takeoff angle lets the signal travel farther before reaching the ionosphere and farther again before landing, so each hop covers more distance. Fewer hops are needed for a given path, which also means less ground-reflection loss.
E3B08: Ground-wave signals lose energy to the Earth as they travel, and that loss grows with frequency. So the higher the frequency, the shorter the usable ground-wave range, which is why ground wave is most useful on MF and the lower HF bands.
E3B09: Sporadic-E openings peak around the solstices, with the strongest and most frequent season near the summer solstice. A smaller secondary peak comes around the winter solstice.
E3B10: In chordal-hop propagation the signal bounces along inside the ionosphere without returning to Earth between hops. Skipping those ground reflections avoids their losses, so the signal arrives stronger than a normal multi-hop path.
E3B11: Sporadic-E is mainly a daytime event, most likely between sunrise and sunset, often with a peak late in the morning and another in the late afternoon or early evening. Nighttime openings occur but are less common.
E3B12: Chordal hop is when a signal is refracted from one region of the ionosphere to another, again and again, without coming down to the ground in between. It is not about leaving the great-circle bearing or crossing the geomagnetic equator.
E3B13: Ground waves need vertical polarization, because horizontally polarized waves near the ground are largely shorted out by the Earth. That is why AM broadcast and other ground-wave services use vertical antennas.
E3C01: A solar flare sends out X-rays that reach Earth in about 8 minutes and sharply raise D-layer ionization on the sunlit side, absorbing HF signals and causing a sudden, short blackout. A coronal mass ejection takes a day or more to arrive.
E3C02: The A-index and K-index measure how disturbed Earth's magnetic field is, so a rising value means more geomagnetic disturbance. They do not measure solar UV or the critical frequency.
E3C03: When the geomagnetic field is disturbed, charged particles pour into the polar regions, ionizing the auroral oval and causing heavy absorption there. Paths that cross the auroral zone suffer most, while transequatorial and NVIS paths are far less affected.
E3C04: Bz is the north-south component of the interplanetary magnetic field carried by the solar wind. Space-weather reports give it because its direction controls how much solar wind energy enters Earth's magnetosphere.
E3C05: When Bz points south it is opposite to Earth's northward field, so the two connect and let solar wind particles and energy into the magnetosphere, raising the chance of storms. A northward Bz mostly keeps them out.
E3C06: The lower atmosphere bends VHF and UHF waves slightly back toward Earth, so the radio horizon is roughly 15 percent farther than the geometric horizon. The usual model treats Earth's radius as 4/3 as large, and the square root of 4/3 is about 1.15.
E3C07: Solar flares are graded A, B, C, M and X, with each class ten times stronger in X-ray output than the one before. X-class flares are the most intense. There is no Class Z.
E3C08: NOAA rates geomagnetic storms G1 through G5, and G5 is the extreme level. Letters such as X and M grade solar flares, not geomagnetic storms.
E3C09: Propagation reporting networks such as the Reverse Beacon Network and PSKReporter log CW and digital-mode signals that receivers decode on the air. They report who was heard where and how well, not solar flux or magnetic data.
E3C10: The 304A parameter is the Sun's ultraviolet output at a wavelength of 304 angstroms, emitted by ionized helium. This UV helps ionize the F layer and tracks closely with the solar flux index.
E3C11: VOACAP, the Voice of America Coverage Analysis Program, predicts HF skywave propagation. It estimates which frequencies and times will work between two points from the solar activity, the date and the antennas.
E3C12: A sudden jump in background noise across much of HF suggests that a solar flare or the arrival of a coronal mass ejection has disturbed the ionosphere and geomagnetic field. A temperature inversion affects VHF and up, not wideband HF noise.
E4A01: A digital scope can only represent signals below half its sampling rate, the Nyquist limit, so the sampling rate of its analog-to-digital converter sets the highest frequency it can show accurately. The circuit's Q has nothing to do with it.
E4A02: A spectrum analyzer shows signal amplitude on the vertical axis against frequency on the horizontal axis. That frequency-domain view is what separates it from an oscilloscope, which plots amplitude against time.
E4A03: A spectrum analyzer displays every signal across a range of frequencies, so spurs and intermodulation products next to the SSB signal show up as separate peaks. A logic analyzer reads digital states and cannot show RF products.
E4A04: To compensate a scope probe you feed it a square wave, usually from the scope's calibrator output, and adjust its small trimmer capacitor until the flat tops and bottoms are neither rounded nor peaked. A flat square wave means the probe passes all frequencies evenly.
E4A05: A prescaler divides the input frequency by a known factor so a high-frequency signal falls within the counter's range, and the reading is then scaled back up. It lowers the frequency, it does not multiply it.
E4A06: When a signal is sampled too slowly, the samples trace out a false lower-frequency waveform that may look unstable or jittery on screen. That is aliasing. The vertical calibration and DC offset are not what it affects.
E4A07: An antenna analyzer works out SWR and impedance for you, often across a sweep of frequencies. It does not tune the antenna for you and does not show a modulation envelope.
E4A08: A directional wattmeter, a vector network analyzer and an antenna analyzer can each measure SWR. The wattmeter derives it from forward and reflected power, and the analyzers measure the reflection directly.
E4A09: Keep the probe ground lead as short as you can, because a long ground lead adds inductance that causes ringing and overshoot on fast signals. The other statements are not real rules; high-impedance and DC-coupled probes are used all the time.
E4A10: Ripple on a linear supply comes from the AC mains frequency, so line triggering, which locks the sweep to the AC line, gives a steady trace of it. Edge or level triggering may not lock well on a small, noisy ripple riding on DC.
E4A11: An antenna analyzer can measure a feed line's velocity factor and its length, and it can find the resonant frequency of a tuned circuit. All three come from how impedance changes with frequency.
E4B01: Every frequency counter reading is measured against its internal time base, so any error in that reference shows up directly in the reading. That is why good counters use a temperature-controlled or GPS-disciplined reference oscillator.
E4B02: For an analog meter, input resistance = full-scale voltage x ohms per volt. A 20,000 ohms per volt meter on its 10 V range presents 10 x 20,000 = 200,000 ohms, so a higher rating loads the circuit less.
E4B03: In S parameter notation the first subscript is the output port and the second the input port, so S21 compares the signal leaving port 2 with the signal entering port 1. That ratio is the forward gain or transmission.
E4B04: S11 is the signal reflected back out of port 1 compared with the signal sent into port 1. That is the input reflection coefficient, which gives return loss and VSWR. S22 is the same thing measured at the output port.
E4B05: A vector network analyzer is calibrated with a short circuit, an open circuit and a precise 50 ohm load, the classic short, open and load standards. Each has a known reflection, so the instrument can remove its own errors.
E4B06: Power into the load = forward power - reflected power = 100 W - 25 W = 75 W. Adding the two to get 125 W is the common mistake; the reflected power is returning toward the transmitter, not reaching the load.
E4B07: The two digits after the S name the ports involved: the first is the port where the signal is measured and the second the port where it is applied. They say nothing about timing or data quality.
E4B08: Q of a tuned circuit = resonant frequency / bandwidth between its half-power points. A circuit resonant at 7 MHz with a 70 kHz bandwidth has Q = 7,000 / 70 = 100, so measuring the bandwidth of the response gives Q.
E4B09: A two-port vector network analyzer sweeps a signal through a device and measures what comes out and what reflects, so it can show a filter's frequency response, including loss and phase. Phase noise and pulse rise time need other instruments.
E4B10: The standard two-tone test drives the SSB transmitter with two audio tones that are not harmonically related, then looks at the RF output on a spectrum analyzer. Any intermodulation shows up as extra signals spaced beside the two tones.
E4B11: A vector network analyzer measures both magnitude and phase of reflected and transmitted signals, so it can find input impedance, output impedance and the reflection coefficient. All three are standard measurements.
E4C01: Phase noise on the master clock spreads noise sidebands around every signal the receiver mixes. A strong signal nearby can then mix with those sidebands and drop noise onto the frequency you are listening to, which is reciprocal mixing.
E4C02: A preselector or front-end filter stops strong signals outside the band before they reach the first amplifier or mixer, where they would cause overload. A narrow IF filter only acts after those stages, too late to help.
E4C03: In FM, the stronger of two signals on the same frequency takes over the demodulator output and the weaker one nearly vanishes. This is the capture effect, which is why FM gives either one station clearly or the other.
E4C04: Noise figure is how much noise a receiver adds compared with a perfect, noiseless receiver, expressed in dB. A 3 dB noise figure means the receiver doubles the noise beyond the theoretical minimum. Atmospheric noise is not part of the definition.
E4C05: Thermal noise power = k x T x B. At 290 K in a 1 Hz bandwidth, 1.38 x 10^-23 x 290 x 1 is about 4.0 x 10^-21 W, which is -174 dBm. A perfect receiver at room temperature cannot have a lower noise floor than that.
E4C06: Noise power rises in proportion to bandwidth, so the increase = 10 log(1,000 / 50) = 10 log(20), about 13 dB. Going from 50 Hz to 1,000 Hz lets in 20 times as much noise.
E4C07: MDS stands for minimum discernible signal, the weakest signal the receiver can detect, usually defined as the level that equals its noise floor in a given bandwidth. It is a common sensitivity rating in receiver reviews.
E4C08: An SDR's analog-to-digital converter can only represent voltages up to its reference voltage. Signals that go beyond it clip, which causes distortion and spurious signals across the band. The sample rate has nothing to do with overload.
E4C09: A high IF puts the image frequency far from the wanted signal, since the image sits two times the IF away. A front-end filter can then remove the image easily. A high IF does not by itself improve noise figure or reduce drift.
E4C10: Matching the receive bandwidth to the signal, narrow for CW and wider for SSB, lets in all of the wanted signal while keeping out extra noise and nearby stations. That gives the best signal-to-noise ratio and the least interference.
E4C11: On the low HF bands, atmospheric noise is usually far stronger than the receiver's own noise. An attenuator lowers signal and atmospheric noise together, and that noise still stays above the receiver's noise, so the signal-to-noise ratio barely changes while overload is reduced.
E4C12: A roofing filter is a narrow filter right after the first mixer that keeps strong signals near the receive frequency out of later stages. That raises the receiver's blocking dynamic range. It does not lower front-end noise.
E4C13: In reciprocal mixing, noise from the receiver's local oscillator mixes with a strong signal close to the one you want, putting noise into your passband. The phase noise on the oscillator causes it, not two out-of-band signals combining.
E4C14: IF Shift slides the IF passband up or down relative to the signal without changing the tuned frequency. You can move the filter edge away from a station just beside yours, reducing interference while staying on frequency.
E4D01: Blocking dynamic range is the span in dB from the receiver's noise floor up to the level of an off-frequency signal that causes 1 dB of gain compression. It shows how strong a nearby signal can be before the wanted signal is weakened.
E4D02: With poor dynamic range, strong signals near your frequency overload the front end, causing cross modulation, where their modulation appears on other signals, and desensitization, where weak signals fade. Oscillator stability has nothing to do with it.
E4D03: When two repeater transmitters are close together, each one's signal gets into the other's final amplifier, which is nonlinear, and the two mix. The mixing produces new frequencies that can land on a repeater input or another channel.
E4D04: A circulator at the transmitter output passes the outgoing signal to the antenna but sends energy coming back from the antenna into a terminating load. That keeps a nearby transmitter's signal from reaching the final amplifier and mixing there.
E4D06: Desensitization is the loss of receiver sensitivity when a strong signal near your frequency overloads the front end. Weak signals you could copy before become hard to hear even though nothing transmits on your exact frequency.
E4D07: Adding attenuation before the first RF stage lowers the strong signal to a level the front end can handle, so it stops overloading. Increasing front-end gain would make desensitization worse.
E4D08: Intermodulation happens when signals pass through a nonlinear circuit or device, which creates sum and difference products such as 2f1 - f2. A perfectly linear circuit would pass the signals without mixing them.
E4D09: A preselector is a tuned filter ahead of the receiver that passes the band you are using and rejects signals outside it. It improves image rejection and keeps strong out-of-band signals from overloading the front end.
E4D10: The third-order intercept point is where the extended lines for the wanted output and the third-order products would meet. At 40 dBm, two 40 dBm input signals would in theory produce third-order products as strong as each of the signals.
E4D11: Odd-order products such as 2f1 - f2 fall near the original signals. Two signals at 14.010 and 14.020 MHz give products at 14.000 and 14.030 MHz, still in the band, while even-order products land far away.
E4D12: Received level = 40 + 10 - 3 - 136 = -89 dBm. The level needed is the MDS plus the required SNR, -103 + 6 = -97 dBm. Link margin = -89 - (-97) = +8 dB.
E4D13: Received level = transmit power + transmit antenna gain + receive antenna gain - path loss = 40 + 6 + 3 - 100 = -51 dBm. All the figures are in dB, so they simply add and subtract.
E4D14: P = 1 mW x 10^(-100/10) = 10^-3 x 10^-10 W = 10^-13 W, which is 0.1 picowatt. Each 10 dB below 0 dBm divides the power by ten.
E4E01: An automatic notch filter looks for steady tones and removes them. A CW signal is also a steady tone, so the filter may notch out the station you want along with the interfering carrier. That is why ANF is usually turned off for CW.
E4E02: DSP noise reduction can often lower broadband white noise, ignition noise and power line noise, since it separates signal from noise statistically. How well it works varies, but it can help with each.
E4E03: A noise blanker detects short, strong pulses and mutes the receiver for their brief duration, so it removes impulse noise such as ignition clicks. Continuous noise, hum and buzz carry on between pulses and are not blanked.
E4E04: Ferrite chokes on the charging system leads block the RF noise the alternator and regulator put out while letting DC charging current pass. Capacitors go across leads to bypass noise, never in series, which would block the charging current.
E4E05: A brute-force AC-line filter in series with the motor's power leads blocks the RF noise from the brushes before it travels out on the house wiring. A high-pass filter would pass the RF and is the wrong type.
E4E06: Computer network equipment uses clock and data signals that can radiate, appearing in a receiver as steady carriers, modulated or not, at fixed frequencies, often drifting a little. A whining or clicking noise points to other sources.
E4E07: When common-mode current flows on a cable's shield and conductors together, the whole cable acts like an antenna and can radiate or pick up interference. Low-inductance shield grounds at both ends and braided shields are normal good practice.
E4E08: Common-mode current flows in the same direction and amount on every conductor of a cable, so the cable behaves like a single wire. Differential-mode current is the normal signal, flowing out on one conductor and back on another.
E4E09: A noise blanker reacts to strong pulses, and a very strong nearby signal can trigger it, chopping the signal and creating distortion products that seem to spread across the band. Turning the blanker off clears this up.
E4E10: Arcing thermostat contacts, a faulty doorbell or its transformer, and a failing lighted sign can each produce intermittent loud roaring or buzzing on the AC line. Any arcing in AC wiring can do it.
E4E11: Corroded metal joints can act like crude diodes, so strong local broadcast signals mix in them and the products are reradiated on other frequencies. This is the rusty bolt effect. Over-modulation would not combine two stations.
E4E12: Switch-mode power supplies switch at a fixed rate and produce harmonics at regular spacing, heard as a series of carriers marching across a wide frequency range. Radar and electric fences produce pulses or clicks instead.
E4E13: The surge protector for station AC belongs on the single point ground panel, so that it and every other protector share one ground reference. Bonding them together keeps transients from creating voltage differences between equipment.
E4E14: A single point ground panel bonds every protector, for feed lines, rotator cables and AC, to one common ground. During a lightning surge they all rise to the same potential and activate together, so no damaging voltage builds up between them.
E5A01: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, so only the small resistance limits current. That large current flowing through each reactance develops a voltage across it that can be many times the applied voltage. A low Q would do the opposite and keep those voltages small.
E5A02: f = 1 / (2 x pi x sqrt(L x C)) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x sqrt(50e-6 x 40e-12)) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x 4.472e-8) = 1 / 2.81e-7, about 3.56 MHz. Resistance does not change the resonant frequency, so the 22 ohms is not used.
E5A03: In a series RLC circuit at resonance, XL and XC are equal and opposite, so they cancel. What remains is the circuit resistance, which is why the impedance is at its minimum and roughly equal to R rather than to either reactance.
E5A04: At parallel resonance the inductive and capacitive branch currents are equal and opposite, so the LC combination looks like a very high impedance. The source then sees mainly the resistance, so the impedance magnitude is approximately the circuit resistance.
E5A05: Bandwidth equals the center frequency divided by Q, so raising the Q of a matching network narrows the range of frequencies it matches well. A higher Q network is sharper, not broader, and it tends to suppress harmonics rather than add them.
E5A06: In a parallel LC tank at resonance, energy swings back and forth between the coil and the capacitor, so the current circulating inside the loop is at its maximum, often Q times the line current. The formula involving 2 pi and the square root of LC gives frequency, not current.
E5A07: A parallel resonant circuit presents its highest impedance at resonance, so the current drawn from the source is at a minimum there, even though a large current circulates inside the tank itself.
E5A08: At resonance the reactances cancel and the series circuit acts like a pure resistance, so voltage and current are in phase. A 90 degree shift would mean a purely reactive load, which is not the case at resonance.
E5A09: For a parallel resonant circuit, Q = R / X, where X is the reactance of either the inductor or the capacitor (they are equal at resonance). This is the inverse of the series case, where Q = X / R, which is the tempting wrong choice.
E5A10: f = 1 / (2 x pi x sqrt(L x C)) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x sqrt(50e-6 x 10e-12)) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x 2.236e-8) = 1 / 1.405e-7, about 7.12 MHz. The 33 ohm resistance does not affect the resonant frequency.
E5A11: Half-power bandwidth = f / Q = 7,100,000 Hz / 150 = 47,333 Hz, about 47.3 kHz. Dividing in the wrong direction or mixing up units gives the much smaller hertz values listed.
E5A12: Half-power bandwidth = f / Q = 3,700,000 Hz / 118 = 31,356 Hz, about 31.4 kHz. Half of that, 15.7 kHz, is the distance from center to one half-power point, not the full bandwidth.
E5A13: In a series resonant circuit the voltage across each reactance is about Q times the applied voltage, so raising Q raises those internal voltages. Components must be rated to handle them, which is a practical concern in high-Q tuners and filters.
E5B01: One time constant (R x C seconds) is the time for a capacitor to charge to 63.2% of the applied voltage, or discharge to 36.8% of its starting voltage. After about five time constants it is essentially fully charged or discharged.
E5B02: Susceptance, the imaginary part of admittance, is written with the letter B. G is conductance, Y is admittance as a whole, and X is reactance.
E5B03: Admittance is 1 divided by impedance. In polar form you take the reciprocal of the magnitude and change the sign of the phase angle, so 50 ohms at +30 degrees becomes 0.02 siemens at -30 degrees.
E5B04: Two 220 uF capacitors in parallel give 440 uF, and two 1 megohm resistors in parallel give 0.5 megohm. Time constant = R x C = 500,000 x 0.000440 = 220 seconds.
E5B05: Susceptance is the reciprocal of reactance (B = 1 / X), so converting a pure reactance to susceptance replaces its magnitude with the reciprocal. A 50 ohm reactance becomes 0.02 siemens of susceptance.
E5B06: Admittance is written Y = G + jB, where G is conductance and B is susceptance. Susceptance is therefore the imaginary part of admittance, the reactive counterpart of conductance, measured in siemens.
E5B07: Net reactance = XL - XC = 250 - 500 = -250 ohms, which is capacitive. Angle = arctan(250 / 1000) = 14.0 degrees. Because the circuit is capacitive, the current leads, so the voltage lags the current by 14.0 degrees.
E5B08: Net reactance = XL - XC = 100 - 300 = -200 ohms (capacitive). Angle = arctan(200 / 100) = 63.4 degrees, about 63 degrees. A capacitive circuit has the voltage lagging the current.
E5B09: In a capacitor, current flows to change the charge before the voltage can build, so the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees. The memory aid ELI the ICE man puts I before E for a capacitor (C).
E5B10: An inductor opposes changes in current, so the voltage across it appears first and the current follows, with voltage leading current by 90 degrees. In ELI the ICE man, E comes before I for an inductor (L).
E5B11: Net reactance = XL - XC = 75 - 25 = +50 ohms, which is inductive. Angle = arctan(50 / 100) = 26.6 degrees, about 27 degrees. In an inductive circuit the voltage leads the current.
E5B12: Admittance (Y) is the inverse of impedance, Y = 1 / Z, measured in siemens. It describes how easily AC flows. The inverse of reactance alone is susceptance, which is only the imaginary part of admittance.
E5C01: In rectangular form the real part is resistance and the imaginary part is reactance, with capacitive reactance negative. A pure 100 ohm capacitive reactance has zero resistance, so it is written 0 - j100. Plus j100 would be inductive.
E5C02: Polar coordinates describe an impedance by its magnitude (total ohms) and its phase angle. Real and imaginary parts, or R and X values, are the rectangular way of writing the same impedance.
E5C03: A pure inductive reactance has voltage leading current by a full 90 degrees, so in polar form it sits at a positive 90 degree angle. A negative 90 degree angle would be a pure capacitive reactance, and 45 degrees means equal resistance and reactance.
E5C04: Frequency response plots usually put gain or attenuation on a logarithmic scale, often in decibels, because responses span many orders of magnitude. A linear axis would squeeze the small values near zero.
E5C05: A phasor diagram draws impedances, voltages or currents as arrows whose length is magnitude and whose angle is phase at one frequency. A Venn diagram shows set overlap and has nothing to do with phase.
E5C06: In R + jX notation the real part, 50, is resistance and the imaginary part, -25, is reactance. A negative j term is capacitive, so this is 50 ohms of resistance in series with 25 ohms of capacitive reactance.
E5C07: On rectangular impedance coordinates, resistance is on the horizontal axis and reactance on the vertical axis. A pure resistance has no reactance, so it falls right on the horizontal axis.
E5C08: Polar coordinates show a magnitude and an angle, which makes them a natural way to display the phase angle of a circuit with resistance and reactance. The Maidenhead grid is a locator system for geographic position.
E5C09: When impedance is graphed in rectangular form, the horizontal X axis carries resistance and the vertical Y axis carries reactance, positive for inductive and negative for capacitive. The axes are not magnitude and phase, which belong to polar form.
E5D01: As frequency rises, RF current crowds toward the outer surface of a conductor, so less of the cross section carries it and the effective resistance goes up. That is why RF conductors are often wide straps or plated with silver.
E5D02: Every bit of lead has inductance, and at VHF and higher the reactance of even a short lead (XL = 2 x pi x f x L) becomes significant. Keeping leads short minimizes that unwanted inductive reactance and the coupling it causes.
E5D03: Reactive power exists when current and voltage are 90 degrees out of phase, as in a pure inductor or capacitor. Energy flows in and back out each cycle, so the average power is zero. In-phase current and voltage would be real power.
E5D04: At microwave frequencies a connection only a few millimeters long is a noticeable fraction of a wavelength, so it adds phase shift. Short connections keep that phase shift, and the impedance changes it causes, small.
E5D05: Electrolytic capacitors are built from long rolled foils, giving them substantial series inductance. At RF that inductance dominates, so the part no longer behaves like a capacitor. That is why they are used for power supply and audio bypassing, not RF.
E5D06: The turns of a coil sit side by side with small capacitance between them. That inter-turn capacitance resonates with the coil's own inductance at some frequency, its self-resonant frequency, above which the part acts like a capacitor.
E5D07: Every real component has its intended (nominal) reactance plus unwanted parasitic reactance, such as lead inductance in a capacitor or winding capacitance in a coil. The two resonate together to set the component's self-resonant frequency.
E5D08: Film capacitors use low-loss dielectrics, so at RF most of their loss comes from skin effect raising the resistance of the thin metal plates and leads. Dielectric loss is the tempting choice, but film dielectrics are quite efficient.
E5D09: An ideal inductor stores energy in its magnetic field and an ideal capacitor stores it in its electric field, then each returns that energy to the circuit. No energy is dissipated as heat, so reactive power is not consumed.
E5D10: A thicker conductor has more capacitance along its length, which slows the wave slightly. So its electrical length, measured in wavelengths, increases and a thick antenna element resonates a little lower than a thin one of the same physical length.
E5D11: Only the resistor dissipates real power. P = I squared x R = 1 x 1 x 100 = 100 watts. The 100 ohm inductive reactance stores and returns energy and adds no real power, so 141.4 watts (the apparent power) is wrong.
E5D12: Reactive power is the energy that moves back and forth between a source and inductors or capacitors without being used up, sometimes called wattless or nonproductive power. It is measured in volt-amperes reactive (VAR), not watts.
E6A01: Gallium arsenide has higher electron mobility than silicon, so devices made from it switch faster and add less noise at very high frequencies. That makes GaAs a common choice for microwave amplifiers and receivers.
E6A02: N-type material is doped with donor atoms that have an extra valence electron, giving it excess free electrons as the majority carriers. P-type material instead has an excess of holes.
E6A03: Reverse bias pulls holes in the P side and electrons in the N side away from the junction. That widens the depletion region, which has almost no free carriers, so essentially no current crosses the junction.
E6A04: An acceptor impurity has one fewer valence electron than the semiconductor, so it accepts an electron and leaves a hole, making P-type material. A donor impurity does the opposite and adds free electrons.
E6A05: The gate of an FET is either a reverse-biased junction or insulated by oxide, so it draws almost no DC current and has very high input impedance. A bipolar transistor's base is forward biased and draws current, giving a much lower input impedance.
E6A06: Beta is the common-emitter current gain of a bipolar transistor, the change in collector current divided by the change in base current. A transistor with a beta of 100 changes collector current 100 times as much as base current.
E6A07: A silicon base-emitter junction starts conducting at about 0.6 to 0.7 volts forward bias, so that voltage shows the transistor is turned on. Six or seven volts would exceed the reverse breakdown of many junctions and is not a normal on condition.
E6A08: Alpha is the common (grounded) base current gain. The frequency where alpha falls to about 0.707 of its low-frequency value is the alpha cutoff frequency. Beta cutoff is the matching term for the common-emitter gain.
E6A09: A depletion-mode FET already has a conducting channel, so current flows from source to drain with zero gate voltage. Gate voltage of the proper polarity depletes the channel and reduces current. An enhancement-mode FET is off at zero gate voltage.
E6A12: A MOSFET gate is insulated by a very thin oxide layer that static discharge can puncture. Zener diodes from gate to source or drain clamp any voltage spike before it reaches that layer, protecting the gate from static damage.
E6B01: A Zener diode operated in reverse breakdown holds a nearly constant voltage across it while the current through it varies widely. That makes it useful as a simple voltage reference or regulator.
E6B02: A Schottky diode's metal-semiconductor junction has a forward drop of roughly 0.2 to 0.4 volts, compared with about 0.7 volts for silicon. Less drop means less wasted power and heat in a rectifier. Schottky diodes usually have lower, not higher, reverse breakdown.
E6B03: An LED's forward voltage is set by the band gap of its semiconductor, the energy an electron gives up when it crosses the junction. A wider band gap gives shorter wavelength light and a higher forward voltage, so blue LEDs need more volts than red ones.
E6B04: A varactor diode is built so the width of its reverse-biased depletion region, and so its capacitance, changes with the applied voltage. It works as a voltage-controlled capacitor for tuning and frequency control.
E6B05: A PIN diode has a wide intrinsic layer between its P and N regions, which gives it very low junction capacitance when reverse biased. That keeps RF from leaking through when the switch is off, while forward current lets RF pass when it is on.
E6B06: Schottky diodes have very little stored charge, so they switch extremely fast, which suits them to VHF and UHF mixers and detectors. Negative resistance oscillators use tunnel diodes, and voltage references use Zener diodes.
E6B07: Current through a diode's forward drop produces heat. Too much current raises the junction temperature past its limit and the junction is damaged. Excessive inverse voltage is a different failure, one caused by voltage rather than current.
E6B08: A Schottky barrier diode is formed by a junction of metal against a semiconductor, rather than a PN junction. That structure gives its low forward voltage and fast switching. A PIN junction describes a different diode type.
E6B09: A point-contact diode uses a fine wire touching a semiconductor, giving very low capacitance. That makes it well suited to detecting RF signals, as in crystal radio receivers and RF probes, rather than handling power.
E6B11: The RF resistance of a PIN diode falls as its forward DC bias current rises. Varying that DC current therefore varies how much RF the diode passes or shunts, making it a current-controlled RF attenuator.
E6C01: Hysteresis sets two thresholds, one for rising and one for falling input. A noisy signal hovering near a single threshold would make the output chatter, but with hysteresis the output switches cleanly once and stays put.
E6C02: A comparator compares its input with a threshold. When the input crosses that threshold, the comparator switches its output from one state to the other, high to low or low to high.
E6C03: Tri-state logic outputs can be a 0, a 1, or a third high-impedance state that effectively disconnects them. This lets several devices share one bus, with only the selected device driving it at a time.
E6C04: BiCMOS combines CMOS transistors at the inputs, giving high input impedance and low drive current, with bipolar transistors at the outputs, giving low output impedance and strong drive. It is not immune to static and is generally more costly than plain CMOS.
E6C05: CMOS logic draws almost no current except while switching, because one transistor of each complementary pair is always off. That gives it the lowest power consumption of these families. ECL is fast but draws considerable current all the time.
E6C06: A CMOS input switches at roughly half the supply voltage, leaving wide margins on both sides. Noise has to move the input nearly halfway across the supply range before it causes a false state change.
E6C07: A pull-up or pull-down resistor ties a line to the positive supply or to ground so it sits at a known logic level when nothing is driving it, such as an open switch or a tri-state output. Without it the input could float and read randomly.
E6C09: An FPGA's internal logic is described in a hardware description language such as VHDL or Verilog, then compiled into a configuration file loaded into the chip. Karnaugh maps help simplify small logic expressions but do not configure an FPGA.
E6D01: Piezoelectric materials such as quartz produce a voltage when mechanically stressed and bend or flex when a voltage is applied. This two-way effect is what lets a quartz crystal act as a stable resonator.
E6D02: A quartz crystal behaves like a series RLC circuit, representing its mechanical resonance, in parallel with a shunt capacitance from the electrodes, holder and strays. That gives it both a series and a slightly higher parallel resonant frequency.
E6D03: One aspect of the piezoelectric effect is that applying a voltage mechanically deforms the material. The reverse also occurs, voltage from stress. Deformation from a magnetic field is magnetostriction, a different effect.
E6D04: A changing magnetic field induces circulating eddy currents in a conductive core, wasting power as heat. Building the core from thin insulated laminations breaks up those current paths and greatly reduces eddy current loss.
E6D05: Ferrite materials generally have higher permeability than powdered iron, so a ferrite core reaches a given inductance with fewer turns. Powdered iron usually wins on temperature stability, which is the tempting wrong choice.
E6D06: Inductance depends on the core's permeability, how easily it supports a magnetic field. Higher permeability gives more inductance for the same coil. Permittivity is the electric field property that matters for capacitors.
E6D08: Powdered iron cores keep their magnetic characteristics more stable over temperature than ferrite, which is why they are favored for tuned circuits and oscillators. Brass and aluminum are not magnetic core materials at all.
E6D09: A ferrite bead slipped over a lead adds loss at VHF and UHF while having little effect at HF. Placed at a transistor amplifier's input and output, it damps unwanted high-frequency parasitic oscillations.
E6D10: A toroid is a closed ring, so most of the magnetic field stays inside the core. That reduces coupling to nearby parts and means the coil can be mounted close to other components. Coupling more energy to other parts is the opposite of its advantage.
E6D11: Brass is a nonmagnetic conductor. A changing field induces eddy currents in a brass slug that oppose the coil's field, so inserting it lowers inductance. Ferrite raises inductance because of its high permeability.
E6D12: A core saturates when the magnetic flux, from too much current, reaches the most the material can carry. Beyond that, more current produces little more flux, permeability drops, and inductance falls sharply.
E6E01: Gallium arsenide has much higher electron mobility than silicon, so carriers move faster, devices switch faster, and noise is lower at UHF and microwave frequencies. Higher noise figure would be a drawback, not a benefit.
E6E02: A DIP (dual in-line package) has two rows of pins that pass through holes in the circuit board, making it a through-hole package. PLCC, BGA and SOT packages are surface mount types.
E6E03: Gallium nitride has high electron velocity and a wide band gap, letting MMICs work at the highest frequencies and power levels listed. Silicon nitride and silicon dioxide are insulating layers, not active semiconductor material.
E6E04: Most MMICs are designed with 50 ohm input and output impedance, so they drop straight into standard 50 ohm coax and microstrip systems without extra matching. 75 ohms is common in TV and video work, not typical MMICs.
E6E05: Noise figure is a positive number in dB, and a good low-noise UHF preamplifier is around 0.5 dB, adding very little noise. A negative noise figure is not possible, and dBm is a unit of power, not noise figure.
E6E06: MMICs offer a set amount of gain, a low noise figure, and steady input and output impedance, usually 50 ohms, across a wide frequency range. That makes them easy building blocks from VHF to microwave. Near-infinite gain and very high input impedance describe an op amp.
E6E07: MMICs are usually mounted on circuit boards with microstrip lines, a trace over a ground plane with a controlled impedance such as 50 ohms. Microstrip is easy to build on a board and suits the small size of these devices.
E6E08: The common MMIC has no separate bias pin. DC is fed to the output lead through a resistor, an RF choke or both, which deliver supply current while keeping the RF signal from leaking into the power supply.
E6E09: Surface mount parts have no long leads, so they add the least stray inductance and capacitance above HF. TO-220, axial and radial lead packages all have leads that add parasitic reactance at VHF and higher.
E6E10: Surface mount technology offers all of these advantages: smaller circuit area, shorter board traces, and less parasitic inductance and capacitance because the parts have little or no leads. Together these improve RF performance.
E6E11: DIP stands for dual in-line package, an IC case with two parallel rows of pins on opposite sides. The other expansions given are made up and do not describe the package.
E6E12: The pins of a DIP package and its internal bond wires are relatively long, and at UHF and above that lead length adds significant inductance and capacitance. Excessive lead length, not the epoxy or dielectric, is what rules it out.
E6F01: In a photovoltaic cell, electrons in the semiconductor absorb the energy of incoming light. Freed electrons and the holes they leave are swept apart by the junction field, producing current. Photons carry the energy; they are not what absorbs it.
E6F02: Light striking a photoconductive material frees additional charge carriers, so its resistance decreases. A photocell in a night light, for example, drops in resistance as the room gets brighter.
E6F03: The usual optoisolator pairs an LED with a phototransistor in one sealed package. The LED's light switches the phototransistor, passing the signal across with no electrical connection between the two sides.
E6F04: The photovoltaic effect is the direct conversion of light into electrical energy, the principle behind solar cells. A photodiode giving off light is the opposite process, which is what an LED does.
E6F05: An optical shaft encoder detects rotation by shining a light through, or off, a wheel with a pattern of slots or marks. As the shaft turns, the interrupted light produces pulses that show position, direction or speed, as in a radio's tuning knob.
E6F06: Photoconductive devices are most commonly made from crystalline semiconductor material, whose resistance falls when light frees charge carriers. Argon is an inert gas and the other listed material is not a photoconductor.
E6F07: A solid-state relay uses semiconductors, such as an optoisolator driving a triac or MOSFET, to do the job of an electromechanical relay with no moving contacts. A transistor driving a mechanical relay coil is still a mechanical relay.
E6F08: An optoisolator passes the control signal as light, so there is no electrical path between the low-voltage control circuit and the 120 VAC circuit it switches. That isolation protects the control circuit and the user from line voltage.
E6F09: Efficiency of a photovoltaic cell is the fraction of the incoming light energy that it converts into electrical output. Ratios of RF power, lumens or voltage to current describe other things entirely.
E6F10: Silicon is by far the most common material in power-generating solar cells because it is plentiful, well understood and reasonably efficient. Selenium and cadmium sulfide appear in older or light-sensing devices.
E6F11: A single fully illuminated silicon photovoltaic cell produces about 0.5 volts open circuit, so solar panels connect many cells in series to reach useful voltages. The 0.7 volt figure is the forward drop of a silicon diode, the tempting mix-up.
E7A01: A flip-flop has two stable states and stays in whichever one it was last set to until a new input changes it, so it is bistable. AND and OR gates simply follow their inputs and hold no state of their own.
E7A02: A decade counter counts ten input pulses and then resets, giving one output pulse for every ten in, so it divides by 10. Decoding numbers for a seven-segment display is the job of a separate decoder chip.
