E7A03: A toggle-wired flip-flop changes state once per input pulse, so its output completes one full cycle for every two input pulses, halving the frequency. An XOR or OR gate has no memory and cannot count pulses.
E7A04: Each flip-flop divides by 2, so n stages divide by 2 to the power n. For 16: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16, which takes 4 flip-flops. Using 16 flip-flops would divide by 2^16 = 65,536.
E7A05: An astable multivibrator has no stable state, so it keeps flipping between its two states on its own and works as a free-running square wave oscillator. A monostable needs a trigger, and J-K and T flip-flops need a clock or input.
E7A06: A monostable multivibrator rests in one stable state. A trigger pushes it into its other state for a time set by an RC network, then it returns on its own. That is why it is called a one-shot.
E7A07: NAND is an AND gate with its output inverted. AND gives a 1 only when every input is 1, so NAND gives a 0 only in that case and a 1 for every other input combination.
E7A08: An OR gate outputs 1 whenever at least one input is 1, and outputs 0 only when every input is 0. Requiring all inputs to be 1 would describe an AND gate instead.
E7A09: An exclusive OR gives 1 when exactly one input is 1. The exclusive NOR inverts that, so it gives 0 when one and only one input is 1 and gives 1 when both inputs match. It works as an equality detector.
E7A10: A truth table lists every combination of inputs to a digital device and the output each combination produces. It describes logic gates and similar circuits, not op-amps, which are analog.
E7A11: Positive logic means the higher voltage level stands for a logic 1 and the lower level for a logic 0. Negative logic reverses that assignment. It has nothing to do with noise immunity.
E7B01: Class AB bias sits between Class B and Class A, so each device conducts a little longer than half the cycle but not all of it: more than 180 but less than 360 degrees. The overlap reduces crossover distortion compared to Class B.
E7B02: A Class D amplifier drives its output devices as switches, fully on or fully off, using pulse width modulation or similar methods. Little power is lost in a device that is saturated or cut off, so efficiency is high.
E7B03: A switching amplifier's output is close to a square wave, which is rich in harmonics. A low-pass or band-pass filter at the output removes that harmonic content so only the wanted frequency reaches the antenna.
E7B04: For Class A, the transistor is biased about halfway between saturation and cutoff so the signal can swing equally up and down without clipping. The device conducts for the full 360 degrees of the cycle.
E7B05: Parasitic suppressors damp unwanted VHF oscillations in the leads and tube or transistor circuit, and neutralization cancels the internal feedback capacitance that can make a stage oscillate. Tuning for maximum power alone does not stop either.
E7B06: In a grounded-grid amplifier the drive is applied to the cathode, which presents a low input impedance, often around 50 to 100 ohms. The grid shields input from output, so neutralizing is rarely needed, but power gain is modest.
E7B07: SSB is an amplitude-varying signal, so it needs a linear amplifier. A Class C stage is very nonlinear, which flattens and distorts the envelope and creates intermodulation products that spread the signal over excessive bandwidth.
E7B08: A switching device wastes little power when fully on (high current but nearly no voltage across it) or fully off (voltage but nearly no current). Since it spends most of its time in saturation or cutoff, losses stay low.
E7B09: An emitter follower has high input impedance, low output impedance and voltage gain just under one, with the output in phase with the input. Phase inversion belongs to the common emitter configuration, not this one.
E7C01: A low-pass Pi-network looks like the Greek letter pi: a capacitor from the input to ground, a second capacitor from the output to ground, and a series inductor bridging them. Series inductance and shunt capacitance both block higher frequencies.
E7C02: Series capacitors pass high frequencies and block low ones, and a shunt inductor shorts low frequencies to ground. Both act together to make the T-network a high-pass filter.
E7C03: A Pi-L network adds a series output inductor after the Pi-network, forming a second low-pass section. That extra section gives greater attenuation of harmonics than a plain Pi-network.
E7C04: A matching network adds reactance of the opposite sign to cancel the load's reactive part, and it transforms the remaining resistance up or down to the value the source wants, such as 50 ohms.
E7C05: A Chebyshev filter trades a small, controlled ripple in the passband for a steeper cutoff than a Butterworth filter of the same order. A Butterworth filter is maximally flat in the passband with a gentler rolloff.
E7C06: An elliptical (Cauer) filter places one or more zeros, or notches, in the stop band, which gives it an extremely sharp transition from pass to stop. The cost is ripple in both the passband and the stop band.
E7C07: A Pi-L network is an ordinary Pi-network followed by an additional series inductor at the output. The added inductor adds harmonic suppression and helps match higher or lower load impedances.
E7C08: A helical filter uses coils inside shielded cavities to form high-Q resonators in a small space, which makes it a common band-pass or notch filter at VHF and UHF. Sallen-Key filters are active audio-range designs.
E7C09: A crystal lattice filter is built from quartz crystals, usually in matched pairs, arranged to give a narrow, steep-sided passband for low-level signals such as an IF stage. The name comes from the circuit layout, not the crystal shape.
E7C10: A repeater duplexer must notch out the transmitter's powerful signal at the nearby receive frequency, often only 600 kHz away on 2 meters. Resonant cavity filters have the very high Q and power handling that job needs.
E7C11: Shape factor is the ratio of a filter's bandwidth at a deep attenuation point, such as 60 dB down, to its bandwidth at a shallow point, such as 6 dB down. The closer it is to 1, the better it rejects adjacent channels.
E7D01: A linear regulator compares the output to a reference and continuously adjusts how much a pass element conducts, acting like a variable resistor, to hold the output voltage constant. Changing a duty cycle is how a switching regulator works instead.
E7D02: A switchmode regulator turns a switch on and off and sends the pulses through an LC filter that averages them. Changing the duty cycle, the fraction of time the switch is on, sets the output voltage.
E7D03: A Zener diode held in reverse breakdown keeps a nearly constant voltage across itself over a wide range of current, so it makes a simple, stable voltage reference. An SCR is a switching device, not a reference.
E7D04: A common three-terminal regulator such as the 78xx series is a series regulator: input, output and ground, with an internal pass transistor in series with the load. It contains the reference, error amplifier and protection in one package.
E7D05: A shunt regulator sits in parallel with the load and draws whatever current is needed to drop the excess voltage across a series resistor, so it loads the unregulated source. A series regulator instead controls current flowing through to the load.
E7D09: Operating time equals capacity divided by average current. For example, a 10 amp-hour battery supplying an average of 2 amps lasts about 10 / 2 = 5 hours. Dividing current by capacity gives an inverted, meaningless result.
E7D10: A switching supply runs its transformer at tens or hundreds of kilohertz instead of 60 Hz. Transformer core size and filter capacitance needed shrink as frequency rises, so the parts are much smaller, lighter and cheaper.
E7D11: Solar panels produce direct current. An inverter converts that DC into AC so it can run ordinary household equipment or feed the power grid. Preventing nighttime discharge is the job of a blocking diode, not an inverter.
E7D12: Dropout voltage is the smallest difference between input and output at which a linear regulator can still hold its output steady. If the input falls closer than that, the output drops out of regulation.
E7D13: The pass element drops the difference between input and output while carrying the load current, so it dissipates P = (Vin - Vout) x Iout. Example: (15 - 12) x 2 A = 6 W. Vout x Iout is the power delivered to the load.
E7D14: Equal resistors across series filter capacitors do all three jobs: they split the voltage evenly between the capacitors, bleed off their charge after power is removed for safety, and present a small minimum load to the supply.
E7D15: A step-start circuit applies power through a resistor at first, which limits the inrush current while large filter capacitors charge gradually. The resistor is then shorted out once the capacitors are mostly charged.
E7E01: A reactance modulator varies the capacitance in an oscillator's tuning circuit with the audio, shifting its frequency to produce FM or PM. It is applied to a low-level local oscillator, not the final amplifier, and later stages multiply the deviation.
E7E02: A reactance modulator, often a varactor or a transistor acting as a variable capacitance, changes the effective capacitance in an oscillator's tuned circuit in step with the audio. That shifts frequency or phase, producing FM or PM rather than AM.
E7E03: A frequency discriminator is an FM detector: it turns changes in the frequency of the incoming signal into changes in output voltage, recovering the audio. It does not generate FM or filter adjacent signals.
E7E04: A balanced modulator produces both sidebands and suppresses the carrier, giving double sideband. A sharp filter then removes one sideband, leaving single sideband. This is the classic filter method.
E7E05: A pre-emphasis network in the transmitter boosts higher audio frequencies before modulation, improving their signal-to-noise ratio. The receiver's de-emphasis network then cuts them back to restore a flat response.
E7E06: Phase modulation inherently gives more deviation to higher audio frequencies, which acts like pre-emphasis. De-emphasis in the receiver rolls those highs back off, so an FM receiver sounds correct on PM transmitters.
E7E07: Baseband is the frequency range of the message signal itself before it modulates a carrier, such as the audio from a microphone or a data stream. It is not the lowest band a transceiver covers.
E7E08: A mixer outputs the two original frequencies plus their sum and their difference. Example: mixing 10 MHz and 1 MHz gives 10, 1, 11 and 9 MHz, and a filter selects the wanted product.
E7E09: When a mixer is overdriven, its nonlinear operation creates many unwanted spurious products at combinations of the input frequencies and their harmonics. These show up as spurs and intermodulation in the output.
E7E10: A diode envelope detector rectifies the RF signal and then an RC filter smooths the result, leaving a voltage that follows the amplitude envelope of an AM signal. Zener breakdown plays no part in it.
E7E11: A product detector mixes the SSB signal with a locally generated carrier (BFO) to recover the audio, replacing the carrier removed at the transmitter. A discriminator is used for FM, not SSB.
E7F01: In a direct-sampling SDR, a fast analog-to-digital converter digitizes the RF signal straight from the antenna, often after filtering and amplification, with no analog mixing against a local oscillator. All tuning and demodulation then happen in software.
E7F02: An adaptive filter continually adjusts its coefficients to tell the random noise apart from the correlated speech and suppress the noise. A Hilbert-transform filter is used to create SSB, not to clean up received noise.
E7F03: A Hilbert-transform filter shifts every frequency component by 90 degrees. Combining the shifted and unshifted signals lets the DSP cancel one sideband and keep the other, the digital version of the phasing method.
E7F04: The DSP creates I and Q versions of the audio that are 90 degrees apart and combines them in quadrature with carrier signals that are also 90 degrees apart. One sideband adds and the other cancels, leaving SSB.
E7F05: By the Nyquist rule, the sample rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal. For audio up to 3 kHz that means at least 6,000 samples per second. Sampling slower causes aliasing.
E7F06: Levels needed = 1 V / 0.001 V = 1,000. Nine bits give 2^9 = 512 levels, which is too few, while 10 bits give 2^10 = 1,024 levels, so 10 bits is the minimum. Eight bits give only 256 levels.
E7F07: A Fast Fourier Transform is an efficient algorithm that takes a block of time-domain samples and computes the frequency content, the basis of an SDR waterfall or spectrum display. The inverse FFT goes the other direction.
E7F08: Decimation lowers the sample rate by keeping only every Nth sample and discarding the rest, which reduces the processing load. It must be preceded by low-pass filtering to avoid aliasing.
E7F09: After decimation the lower sample rate can only represent lower frequencies. Any components above the new Nyquist limit would fold back as false lower-frequency signals, so a low-pass anti-aliasing filter removes them first.
E7F10: A sampler can represent signals up to half its sample rate, so the sample rate sets the widest bandwidth a direct-sampling SDR can receive at once. The number of bits affects dynamic range, not bandwidth.
E7F11: The smallest voltage step an ADC can resolve equals its reference voltage divided by 2 raised to the number of bits. With no external noise, a signal smaller than one step cannot be detected, so reference level and sample width set the floor.
E7F12: A symmetric FIR filter has linear phase, meaning it delays every frequency component by the same amount and preserves waveform shape. FIR filters usually need more taps than IIR filters for a given rolloff, and they do not respond faster to impulses.
E7F13: Taps are the points along a DSP filter's delay line, each holding the sample from one sample period earlier. Each delayed sample is multiplied by a coefficient and summed to form the output.
E7F14: Adding taps lets the filter use more delayed samples and coefficients, which allows steeper skirts and a sharper response at the cost of more computation and delay. Lowering Q would broaden the response instead.
E7G01: An op-amp's output impedance is very low, close to zero ohms in the ideal case, especially with negative feedback applied. That lets it drive loads without its output voltage sagging.
E7G02: A capacitor across the feedback resistor lowers the feedback impedance as frequency rises, which reduces the stage gain at higher frequencies. Low frequencies still see the full resistor, so the circuit becomes a low-pass filter.
E7G03: An op-amp's input impedance is very high, ideally infinite, so it draws almost no current from the signal source. Low input impedance would load down the previous stage.
E7G04: Input offset voltage is the small DC voltage that must be applied between the two inputs to bring the open-loop output to zero. It exists because the input transistors are never perfectly matched.
E7G05: High gain and high Q both make an active filter more prone to ringing and instability. Keeping both gain and Q modest gives a stable filter that does not ring on transients.
E7G06: Gain-bandwidth is the frequency at which the op-amp's open-loop gain falls to one. Gain times bandwidth stays about constant, so a part with a 1 MHz figure set for a gain of 10 has roughly 1 MHz / 10 = 100 kHz of bandwidth.
E7G08: An ideal op-amp is defined to have infinite gain at every frequency, so its gain does not vary with frequency. Real op-amps lose gain as frequency rises, but the ideal model ignores that.
E7G12: An operational amplifier is a high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance. External feedback components set its actual circuit gain and response.
E7H01: The Colpitts, Hartley and Pierce circuits are three classic oscillator types. Colpitts uses a capacitive divider for feedback, Hartley a tapped coil, and Pierce a quartz crystal. Taft, Fenner and Beane are not oscillator circuits.
E7H02: A microphonic is an unwanted frequency change in an oscillator caused by mechanical vibration or shock, which physically moves its components and shifts their inductance or capacitance. It can show up as a warble on the signal.
E7H03: A phase-locked loop is a servo loop. A phase detector compares a voltage-controlled oscillator with a stable reference, and a low-pass filter turns the error into a control voltage that keeps the VCO locked in phase.
E7H04: A Colpitts oscillator takes its positive feedback from a capacitive voltage divider, two capacitors in series across the tank circuit. A tapped coil is the feedback method of the Hartley oscillator.
E7H05: In a Pierce oscillator the quartz crystal sits in the feedback path and supplies the positive feedback at its resonant frequency. That gives the Pierce oscillator excellent frequency stability.
E7H06: A phase-locked loop can generate many stable frequencies from one reference by dividing the VCO output in the loop, which is frequency synthesis. Its control voltage tracks an incoming FM signal, so it can demodulate FM too.
E7H07: Because vibration moves parts and shifts the frequency, the fix is to mechanically isolate the oscillator, for example with shock mounts or by keeping it rigid and apart from a vibrating enclosure. NP0 capacitors address temperature drift instead.
E7H08: NP0 (also called C0G) capacitors have a near-zero temperature coefficient, so their value barely changes as they warm up. Using them in an oscillator's tuning reduces thermal drift.
E7H09: A direct digital synthesizer uses a phase accumulator stepping through a lookup table of waveform values, a DAC to turn those values into voltage, and a low-pass filter to remove sampling images. A PLL instead uses a VCO and phase detector.
E7H10: The DDS lookup table stores amplitude values for points around one cycle of the desired waveform, usually a sine wave. The phase accumulator selects which value to send to the DAC at each clock tick.
E7H11: A DDS's main spectral impurities are discrete spurious signals, caused by phase truncation, DAC quantization and nonlinearity, and clock images. They appear as narrow spurs rather than as broadband noise.
E7H12: A crystal's parallel resonant frequency depends on the capacitance across it, so the maker calibrates it for a specified load capacitance. Supplying that capacitance makes the oscillator run on the marked frequency.
E7H13: All three methods are used at microwave frequencies: locking to a GPS-disciplined reference, using a rubidium atomic standard, and using a temperature-controlled high-Q dielectric resonator all give high accuracy and stability.
E8A01: Fourier analysis breaks any repeating waveform into a sum of sine waves at the fundamental and its harmonics. Applied to a square wave, it shows a fundamental plus only odd harmonics, each with amplitude falling as 1/n.
E8A02: A successive approximation converter compares the input against a DAC output one bit at a time, from the most significant bit down, homing in on the digital value. The other listed terms are not ADC methods.
E8A03: A time-domain view, such as an oscilloscope trace, plots signal amplitude against time. A frequency-domain view, like a spectrum analyzer, instead plots amplitude against frequency.
E8A04: Dither is a small amount of random noise added to the ADC input so that low-level signals cross quantization steps randomly. This spreads the quantization error into broadband noise instead of harmonic distortion.
E8A05: A true-RMS meter computes the heating value of the waveform directly, so it reads correctly for square waves, pulses and noise as well as sine waves. Average-responding meters are only accurate for pure sine waves.
E8A06: Normal speech has brief peaks and long low-level stretches, so the peak envelope power of unprocessed SSB voice runs roughly 2.5 times the average power. Speech processing raises the average and shrinks that ratio.
E8A07: In SSB the RF envelope follows the voice, so the peak-to-average ratio is set by how speech varies in loudness, with peaks, pauses and syllable dynamics. Carrier suppression and amplifier gain do not change that ratio.
E8A08: A direct or flash ADC compares the input against all reference levels at once, so it converts extremely fast. That speed lets an SDR sample RF signals directly. Flash converters actually draw a lot of power, so low power is not their benefit.
E8A09: An n-bit converter can output 2^n distinct codes. With 8 bits that is 2^8 = 256 levels. Input amplifier gain changes which voltages map to each code, not how many codes exist.
E8A10: A DAC output is a stepped waveform that carries images and artifacts near multiples of the sample rate. A low-pass reconstruction filter removes those artifacts and leaves a smooth analog signal.
E8A11: Total harmonic distortion shows how faithfully a converter reproduces a pure tone, so it is a standard measure of ADC quality. Peak envelope power and power factor describe transmitters and loads, not converters.
E8B01: FM modulation index is the peak frequency deviation divided by the modulating signal frequency. A larger index means more significant sidebands and a wider signal.
E8B02: Modulation index depends only on deviation and the modulating frequency. The carrier frequency itself plays no part, so a PM signal has the same index whether it is on 2 meters or 10 meters.
E8B03: Modulation index = deviation / modulating frequency = 3000 Hz / 1000 Hz = 3. Dividing the other way gives 0.33, a common mistake.
E8B04: Modulation index = deviation / modulating frequency = 6 kHz / 2 kHz = 3. Using the total swing of 12 kHz would wrongly give 6.
E8B05: Deviation ratio = maximum deviation / highest modulating frequency = 5 kHz / 3 kHz = 1.67. Inverting the ratio gives 0.6, which is wrong.
E8B06: Deviation ratio = maximum deviation / highest modulating frequency = 7.5 kHz / 3.5 kHz = 2.14. The inverted value, 0.47, is a common error.
E8B07: OFDM spreads data across many closely spaced subcarriers and is used by amateur digital modes and high-speed data links. It is a legal and common digital technique on the ham bands.
E8B08: OFDM sends data on many subcarriers spaced so each is orthogonal to the others. That spacing lets them overlap without interfering, and slow symbols on each carrier resist intersymbol interference from multipath.
E8B09: Deviation ratio is the maximum carrier deviation divided by the highest audio modulating frequency the system allows. It is the worst-case modulation index used to size an FM channel.
E8B10: Frequency division multiplexing splits the available bandwidth into separate subbands, each carrying its own data stream at the same time. Jumping between bands would be frequency hopping, not FDM.
E8B11: Time division multiplexing gives each signal its own repeating time slot in one data stream, so several channels share a link by taking turns. Separate subcarriers would be frequency division instead.
E8C01: QAM sends data by amplitude modulating two carriers of the same frequency that are 90 degrees apart, called I and Q. Each symbol is a combination of amplitude and phase, which packs several bits per symbol.
E8C02: Symbol rate is how often the transmitted waveform changes state to carry information, measured in symbols or baud per second. It is not a count of characters or control codes.
E8C03: Shifting a PSK signal's phase when the RF passes through zero avoids a sudden jump in amplitude. Abrupt transitions create wide sidebands, so switching at zero crossings keeps the signal narrow.
E8C04: PSK31 shapes each phase reversal with a smooth sinusoidal amplitude envelope instead of a hard switch. That gentle shaping keeps sidebands tight, giving the mode its roughly 31 Hz bandwidth.
E8C05: A common rule estimates CW bandwidth at about 4 times the speed in words per minute: 13 WPM x 4 = 52 Hz. Clean keying with proper rise and fall times keeps the signal near that width.
E8C06: An FT8 signal uses 8-tone frequency shift keying with tones 6.25 Hz apart, so it occupies about 50 Hz. Many FT8 stations fit side by side within a single 3 kHz audio passband.
E8C07: FSK bandwidth = (K x shift) + baud rate, with K = 1.2. So BW = (1.2 x 4800) + 9600 = 5760 + 9600 = 15,360 Hz, or 15.36 kHz. Using the shift or baud rate alone understates the width.
E8C08: ARQ (automatic repeat request) checks each received block for errors and, if one is found, asks the sender to transmit that block again. Forward error correction, by contrast, fixes errors without a resend.
E8C09: In Gray code, consecutive values differ by only one bit, which avoids large errors when a value is read during a transition, as in shaft encoders. Binary coded decimal and ASCII can change several bits at once.
E8C10: A more efficient code, such as one carrying more bits per symbol or using variable-length characters, moves more data in the same symbol rate and bandwidth. Adding forward error correction uses capacity rather than adding it.
E8C11: Baud is the unit for symbol rate: one baud equals one symbol per second. The bit rate can differ from the baud rate when each symbol carries several bits, but baud and symbol rate are the same thing.
E8C12: CW bandwidth depends on how fast you send and how sharply each element turns on and off. Faster keying and steeper rise and fall times both widen the signal. Receiver IF bandwidth and Q do not affect what is transmitted.
E8C13: A constellation diagram plots each allowed symbol as a point on the I/Q plane, where distance from center is amplitude and angle is phase. It shows every possible phase and amplitude state of a QAM or QPSK symbol.
E8C14: Amateur mesh networks such as AREDN carry ordinary internet protocol traffic, so each node is identified by an IP address. Talk groups belong to digital voice systems, not mesh data networks.
E8C15: Mesh nodes find their neighbors with discovery protocols and then set up links and routes automatically, so the network forms and heals itself. Store-and-forward digipeating is a packet radio technique, not mesh formation.
E8D01: A spread spectrum receiver despreads only the signal using the matching code or hop sequence. Any other signal gets spread out by that process and falls to a low level, so interference is suppressed.
E8D02: Direct sequence spread spectrum uses a fast pseudorandom bit stream to shift the carrier's phase, spreading the signal across a wide bandwidth. Frequency hopping instead moves the carrier between channels.
E8D03: Frequency hopping moves the carrier rapidly among many frequencies in a pseudorandom pattern known to both ends. The receiver follows the same pattern, so a narrow interferer only hits a few hops.
E8D04: Keying a CW signal on or off too abruptly creates wide sidebands heard as clicks on nearby frequencies. These key clicks are near the operating frequency, not harmonics at multiples of it.
E8D05: Slowing the rise and fall of each keyed element, often with a shaping network, narrows the signal and removes key clicks. Making the edges faster would worsen them, and output filters cannot remove nearby sidebands.
E8D06: A parity bit makes the count of 1 bits in each character even or odd, so the receiver can spot a single flipped bit. It detects some errors but cannot correct them and adds no speed.
E8D07: Driving the transmitter with too much audio pushes the AFSK signal into distortion, producing extra tones and splatter. Keeping audio below the point where ALC acts avoids overmodulation.
E8D08: Intermodulation distortion measures the unwanted products created when the AFSK or PSK tones are overdriven. Excess audio raises IMD, which widens the signal and degrades decoding.
E8D09: An idling PSK31 signal is two tones, and a clean transmitter keeps the third-order IMD products about 30 dB or more below them. Readings like -20 dB show overdriven audio and splatter.
E8D10: Baudot uses 5 data bits per character and relies on letters and figures shift codes to double its small character set. ASCII uses 7 or 8 bits, so it has room for every character without shift codes.
E8D11: ASCII has enough code values to carry both uppercase and lowercase letters plus symbols, unlike 5-bit Baudot. It has no built-in error correction, and it needs no shift character.
E9A01: An isotropic radiator is an imaginary lossless antenna that radiates equally in every direction. It cannot be built, but it serves as the reference for gain figures quoted in dBi.
E9A02: Add the decibels first: net gain = 7 dBd - 2 dB - 2.2 dB = 2.8 dB. ERP = 150 W x 10^(2.8/10) = 150 x 1.905 = about 286 watts. Forgetting the duplexer loss gives too high a figure.
E9A03: Effective radiated power combines transmitter output with all feed line and component losses and the antenna gain to give the power effectively sent in the favored direction.
E9A04: Height above ground changes how ground reflections couple back to the antenna, which shifts its feed point impedance. Feed line length and tuner settings change what the radio sees, not the antenna's own impedance.
E9A05: Ground gain is the boost in signal strength in certain directions when waves reflected from the ground add in phase with direct radiation. It depends on antenna height and ground characteristics.
E9A06: Add the decibels first: net gain = 10 dBd - 4 - 3.2 - 0.8 dB = 2 dB. ERP = 200 W x 10^(2/10) = 200 x 1.585 = about 317 watts. Using the antenna gain alone would wrongly give 2,000 watts.
E9A07: Add the decibels first: net gain = 7 dBi - 2 - 2.8 - 1.2 dB = 1 dB. EIRP = 200 W x 10^(1/10) = 200 x 1.259 = about 252 watts. EIRP uses dBi gain, so no dipole correction is needed.
E9A08: Fresnel zone radius shrinks with shorter wavelength, roughly in proportion to the square root of wavelength. 5.8 GHz has the shortest wavelength of the bands listed, so its first Fresnel zone is the smallest.
E9A09: Antenna efficiency is radiation resistance divided by total resistance, where total resistance includes ground, conductor and loading coil losses. Only power in the radiation resistance becomes radiated signal.
E9A10: A ground-mounted vertical's return current flows through the soil, which is lossy. A system of radials gives that current a low-loss path, cutting ground loss and raising efficiency.
E9A11: Return currents for a ground-mounted vertical flow through the earth near the antenna, so soil conductivity sets how much power is lost as heat. Poorly conducting soil means higher ground loss.
E9A12: A half-wave dipole has 2.15 dB gain over isotropic. Gain in dBd = gain in dBi - 2.15 = 6 - 2.15 = 3.85 dBd. Adding instead of subtracting would give the wrong value of 8.15 dB.
E9B07: Gain only redirects power; it does not create any. A lossless directional antenna and an isotropic radiator fed the same power radiate the same total power, the directional one simply concentrates it.
E9B08: The far field begins several wavelengths out, where the pattern shape stays the same as distance grows and field strength simply falls off with distance. Closer in, the reactive near field distorts it.
E9B09: Antenna modeling programs such as NEC and MININEC use the Method of Moments, which solves for current along the antenna wires. From those currents they compute patterns, gain and impedance.
E9B10: Method of Moments divides each wire into short segments and treats each segment as carrying a uniform current, then solves for all the segment currents together. More segments give a finer result.
E9B11: With too few segments the program cannot represent the current distribution accurately, so results such as feed point impedance can be wrong. About 10 segments per half wavelength is a common minimum.
E9C01: With half-wave spacing and 180-degree phasing, signals cancel broadside and add along the line joining the verticals. The result is a figure-eight pattern pointing along the array axis, called end-fire.
E9C02: Quarter-wave spacing with 90-degree phasing makes signals add in one direction along the axis and cancel in the other. The result is a cardioid with a single deep null off the back.
E9C03: Fed in phase and spaced a half wavelength, the two verticals add broadside and cancel along the line joining them. That gives a figure-eight pattern broadside to the array axis.
E9C04: As an unterminated long wire grows to more wavelengths, it develops more lobes, and the main lobes tilt closer to the direction of the wire itself. They do not move toward broadside.
E9C05: Moving the feed point toward one end puts it where the impedance is moderate and similar on the fundamental and several harmonics. That lets one OCFD and a balun cover multiple bands with a usable match.
E9C06: A terminating resistor at the far end absorbs the wave that would otherwise reflect and radiate backward. The antenna then has a traveling wave in one direction only, turning a bidirectional pattern into a unidirectional one.
E9C07: Folding a half-wave dipole with two equal conductors multiplies its feed point impedance by 4: about 73 x 4 = roughly 300 ohms. That is why folded dipoles pair well with 300-ohm twin lead.
E9C08: A folded dipole is a half-wave dipole with a second parallel conductor joining its two ends, forming a narrow loop. The feed goes to one conductor at the center, and the doubled current raises the impedance.
E9C09: The G5RV is a center-fed wire with a specific length of open-wire or ladder line acting as a matching section, which then connects through a balun to coax. It is used as a multiband antenna with a tuner.
E9C10: A Zepp is a half-wave dipole fed at one end, originally through ladder line, a design once used on Zeppelin airships. It is not a phased array or a satellite antenna.
E9C11: Seawater is a far better conductor than soil, so ground reflections near a vertical are much stronger and less lossy. That strengthens the low-angle part of the pattern, which favors long-distance contacts.
E9C12: An extended double Zepp is a center-fed dipole about 1.25 wavelengths long. That length gives more gain broadside than a half-wave dipole, while keeping the pattern from breaking into many lobes.
E9C13: Raising a horizontal antenna higher changes how ground reflections combine, which lowers the takeoff angle of its lowest lobe. Lower takeoff angles favor long-distance HF propagation.
E9C14: Over a downhill slope the ground effectively falls away in front of the antenna, which tilts the main lobe lower toward the horizon in that direction. The takeoff angle in the downhill direction decreases.
E9D01: A dish's gain rises with the square of frequency for a fixed size. Doubling frequency multiplies gain by 4, and 10 x log10(4) = 6.02, about 6 dB.
E9D02: Two Yagis mounted at right angles on one boom, with driven elements at the same point and fed 90 degrees apart, produce circular polarization. The 90-degree phase shift between perpendicular fields makes the field rotate.
E9D03: Placing the loading coil near the middle of a short whip lets more current flow in the lower radiating section than a base coil allows. That raises radiation resistance and efficiency.
E9D04: A loading coil with a high reactance-to-resistance ratio (high coil Q) adds the needed inductance while wasting little power as heat in its resistance. That maximizes antenna efficiency.
E9D05: A Yagi's driven element is a dipole, close to a half wavelength long at the operating frequency. The 234 divided by frequency formula gives a quarter wave in feet, which fits a vertical, not a dipole.
E9D06: Loading coils let a short antenna resonate, but the antenna's Q goes up. Higher Q means the match holds over a narrower range, so SWR bandwidth decreases.
E9D07: A top hat or other top loading keeps current higher along the full vertical section, which raises radiation resistance. Less loading coil inductance is needed, so losses fall and efficiency improves.
E9D08: Higher antenna Q means the impedance changes more quickly as you move away from resonance. The range of frequencies with an acceptable SWR therefore gets narrower.
E9D09: An electrically short antenna has capacitive reactance at its feed point. A loading coil adds inductive reactance that cancels it, bringing the antenna to resonance.
E9D10: Below resonance a whip is electrically shorter than a quarter wave, and radiation resistance drops quickly as electrical length shrinks. That makes losses a larger share of total resistance.
E9D11: With typical spacing, a driven element plus reflector gives a bit more forward gain than a driven element plus director. That is why most two-element Yagis use a reflector.
E9D12: Making a parasitic element longer or shorter than resonance controls the phase of the current induced in it. A longer element acts as a reflector and a shorter one as a director, shaping gain and pattern.
E9E01: In a beta or hairpin match, the hairpin is connected across a split driven element, so each half must be insulated from the boom. Gamma and T matches attach to a continuous element that can be grounded to the boom.
E9E02: A gamma match ties the coax shield to the element's center and the inner conductor to a rod that taps the element a short distance to one side. A series capacitor then tunes out the rod's inductance.
E9E03: A stub match uses a short section of transmission line, open or shorted, connected in parallel with the feed line near the load. Its reactance cancels the load reactance to give a match.
E9E04: The gamma rod adds inductive reactance in series with the feed. The series capacitor cancels that reactance so the match presents a resistive load to the coax.
E9E05: A hairpin acts as a shunt inductor, so it needs a driven element that is slightly short and therefore capacitive. The hairpin's inductance cancels that reactance and steps up the low resistance.
E9E06: A quarter-wave matching section needs Z = square root of (Z1 x Z2) = square root of (100 x 50) = 70.7 ohms. Common 75-ohm coax is the closest suitable value.
E9E07: The reflection coefficient expresses how much of the wave is reflected where a line meets its load, based on the mismatch between them. Characteristic impedance describes the line alone.
E9E08: A Wilkinson divider splits power equally between two 50-ohm outputs while keeping a 50-ohm input match and isolating the outputs from each other. It has nothing to do with dividing frequency.
E9E09: A grounded tower can be fed as a vertical by running a gamma rod up its side, with the coax shield at the base and the center conductor to the rod through a capacitor. Hairpin and double-bazooka matches do not apply.
E9E11: Feeding several driven elements through phasing lines controls the relative phase of their currents, which sets where their fields add and cancel. That shapes the radiation pattern and its direction.
E9F01: Velocity factor is the speed of a wave in the transmission line divided by the speed of light in a vacuum. Solid polyethylene coax is about 0.66, while open-wire line is close to 1.
E9F02: The insulating dielectric slows the wave; velocity factor is about 1 divided by the square root of the dielectric constant. Line length and impedance do not set it.
E9F03: Waves travel more slowly in coax because of its dielectric, so more wavelengths fit in a given physical length. The electrical length is therefore longer than the physical length.
E9F04: A half-wave line repeats its load impedance at the input. A short at the far end therefore appears as a very low impedance to the generator.
E9F05: Microstrip is a printed circuit trace above a ground plane, with width and board material chosen to give a controlled impedance. It acts as a transmission line for microwave circuits.
E9F06: Half wavelength = 300 / f / 2 = 299.8 / 14.10 / 2 = about 10.6 meters. Air-insulated line has a velocity factor near 1, so physical and electrical length are nearly equal.
E9F07: Parallel conductor line with mostly air between its wires has much lower loss than coax with a plastic dielectric, especially at high SWR. It also has a higher velocity factor.
E9F08: Each listed difference holds: foam coax has a higher velocity factor, lower loss per unit length because less plastic dielectric absorbs energy, and a lower maximum safe voltage because foam breaks down more easily.
E9F09: A quarter-wave line inverts its load impedance. A short at the far end appears as a very high impedance at the input, which is why quarter-wave shorted stubs act like parallel tuned circuits.
E9F10: A shorted line less than a quarter wave long looks like an inductor at its input. At one-eighth wave its reactance equals the line's characteristic impedance, inductive.
E9F11: An open line less than a quarter wave long acts like a capacitor at its input. At one-eighth wave its reactance equals the characteristic impedance, capacitive.
E9F12: A quarter-wave line inverts its load. An open far end therefore appears as a very low impedance at the input, like a series tuned circuit.
E9G01: A Smith chart maps impedance and lets you track how it changes moving along a transmission line. It does not handle radiation patterns, radiation resistance or propagation.
E9G02: A Smith chart uses circles of constant resistance and arcs of constant reactance. Every impedance falls where one resistance circle and one reactance arc cross.
E9G03: Smith charts are used to find impedance and SWR at any point on a transmission line, and to design matching networks. They are not used for bearings, patterns or propagation.
E9G04: The two coordinate families on a Smith chart are resistance circles and reactance arcs. Inductance and capacitance appear only as positive and negative reactance values.
E9G05: A common Smith chart task is finding where to place a matching stub on a line and how long to make it. Line impedance from physical dimensions and loss per foot are computed by other methods.
E9G08: Normalizing means dividing every impedance by a reference, usually the line's characteristic impedance, so the chart's prime center represents that value, such as 50 ohms. The scales are not swapped.
E9G09: Constant-SWR circles are centered on the prime center of the Smith chart. Moving along a lossless line keeps you on one such circle, which makes them handy when designing matching networks.
E9G10: The arcs on a Smith chart are lines of constant reactance, inductive above the resistance axis and capacitive below. The full circles are constant resistance.
E9G11: The scales around a Smith chart's rim are marked in fractions of a wavelength along the transmission line, in electrical wavelengths. One full trip around the chart is a half wavelength of line.
E9H01: A Beverage is a long, low wire that works by traveling waves, and it needs to be at least about one wavelength long for useful directivity. Longer Beverages give narrower patterns.
E9H02: On 160 and 80 meters, atmospheric noise is so strong that a lossy receive antenna still hears well above the receiver's own noise. What matters most is directivity to reject noise from other directions.
E9H03: Receiving directivity factor compares an antenna's peak gain in the desired direction to its average gain over the whole hemisphere above it. Higher RDF means better rejection of noise from other directions.
E9H04: An electrostatic shield removes unbalanced capacitive coupling between the loop and nearby objects, which would otherwise fill in the nulls. Keeping the loop balanced gives deeper, sharper nulls for direction finding.
E9H05: A small loop has two nulls 180 degrees apart, so it shows the line a signal lies on but not which side it comes from. Adding a sense antenna resolves that ambiguity.
E9H06: When a Beverage is correctly terminated, the wire behaves like a matched transmission line, so its feed point SWR stays nearly constant across the band. The resistor value giving the least SWR variation is the right one.
E9H07: The resistor sits at the far end of the wire, the end pointed toward the wanted direction. Signals arriving from the reverse direction travel along the wire toward that end, where the resistor absorbs them instead of reflecting them back to the receiver. That gives the Beverage its unidirectional pattern.
E9H08: A sense antenna adds a signal to a loop or other DF antenna, converting its two-null figure-eight into a cardioid with one null. That removes the 180-degree ambiguity in the bearing.
E9H09: A terminated single-turn loop such as the pennant or flag combines a loop response with a dipole-like response, and the termination resistor sets their balance. Adding the two gives a heart-shaped cardioid pattern with one deep null.
E9H10: The voltage induced in a receiving loop is proportional to the number of turns times the area enclosed. Adding turns or making the loop larger raises its output.
E9H11: A cardioid has one deep null in a single direction, so pointing that null at a station gives an unambiguous bearing. A figure-eight pattern has two nulls and leaves the direction uncertain.
